Unit 1: Introduction to Electric Vehicles 1.1 Introduction to Electric Vehicles Road transport is being re-engineered around the electric machine. A vehicle that once relied on a single heat engine and a mechanical gearbox is increasingly a coordinated system of an electrochemical store, power-electronic converters, electric machines, embedded controllers and thermal circuits. This section sets out what an electric vehicle is, how the technology evolved, why it matters, how electrified vehicles are classified, and which components make up the system. The later sections then quantify each of these ideas. 1.1.1 Definition and Concept of Electric Vehicles An electric vehicle (EV) is a road vehicle in which at least part of the propulsive force at the wheels is produced by one or more electric machines drawing energy from an on-board electrical source. The definition is deliberately broad because the source differs among vehicle types: a rechargeable battery, a fuel-cell stack, or a generator driven by an engine. When all the propulsion energy comes from a battery charged from the grid, the vehicle is a pure or battery electric vehicle. Three engineering ideas distinguish an EV from a conventional vehicle. 1. The energy path is mainly electrical. Energy reaches the wheels through cables and converters rather than through a fuel line, combustion chamber and multi-speed gearbox. This allows the designer to place components with much greater freedom. 2. The energy path is bidirectional. An electric machine can act as a motor or as a generator, so kinetic energy can return to the battery during braking. A heat engine has no equivalent ability. 3. The torque source is fast and controllable. A power-electronic drive can change motor torque in milliseconds and can deliver full torque from standstill. Hence many EVs need only a single fixed reduction gear. 1.1.2 Historical Development of Electric Vehicles The EV is older than the petrol car. Its history has three broad phases, an early rise, a long eclipse and a modern return, and each phase was driven by the energy-storage technology available at the time [2, 8]. Early development (1830s–1900). Small electric carriages were demonstrated in the 1830s using non-rechargeable cells. The practical turning point was the lead-acid rechargeable cell of  10

Gaston Planté in 1859, later improved by Camille Fauré’s pasted plates. By the 1890s electric cabs operated in cities such as London and New York. In 1899 the electric car La Jamais Contente of Camille Jenatzy became the first road vehicle to exceed 100 km/h [2]. Decline (1910s–1960s). EVs were quiet, clean and easy to start, but their range was limited by the low specific energy of lead-acid batteries. Three developments favoured petrol vehicles: cheap oil, mass production of the Ford Model T from 1908, and the electric self-starter introduced in 1912, which removed the hand crank. Electric traction then survived mainly in niche roles such as delivery floats, industrial trucks and rail. Renewed interest (1970s–1990s). The oil shocks of the 1970s and later urban air-quality rules revived research. California’s zero-emission vehicle mandate of 1990 prompted vehicles such as the General Motors EV1 (1996), and the Toyota Prius (1997) brought power-split hybrids to mass production [8]. Power MOSFETs, IGBTs and microcontrollers made efficient AC drives possible over the same period. Lithium-ion era (2008 onwards). Lithium-ion cells, first commercialised for portable electronics in 1991, changed the range equation. The Tesla Roadster (2008) and the Nissan Leaf (2010) showed that lithium-ion BEVs were viable, and costs have since fallen with scale. According to the International Energy Agency, global electric-car sales exceeded 20 million in 2025, about one in four new cars sold [27]. In India the Ministry of Heavy Industries’ PM E-DRIVE scheme, with an outlay of Rs 10,900 crore, succeeded FAME-II in 2024 to support electric two- and three-wheelers, buses, trucks and charging infrastructure [28]. 1.1.3 Need and Importance of Electric Mobility The case for electric mobility rests on several linked technical and social drivers. • Energy efficiency. A BEV typically converts about 70–80% of the electrical energy taken from the battery into energy at the wheels, whereas a petrol engine’s tank-to-wheel efficiency in urban use is commonly about 20–25%. Section 1.4 examines these figures. • Local air quality. A BEV has no tailpipe emissions, which matters most in dense cities. Non-exhaust particulates from brakes and tyres remain, although regenerative braking reduces brake wear. • Climate policy. Life-cycle greenhouse-gas emissions depend on the grid mix and on battery manufacture, so the benefit grows as electricity generation decarbonises [29]. • Energy security. Electricity can be generated from domestic and renewable sources, which reduces dependence on imported crude oil. This is significant for India, which imports most of its crude.  11

• Grid and system integration. Parked EVs are a flexible load and, through vehicle-togrid operation, may become a distributed storage resource. • Operating cost and new functionality. Electricity per kilometre is usually cheaper than fuel and there are fewer wearing parts. Precise wheel-torque control also supports stability control and automated driving. 1.1.4 Classification of Electric Vehicles Electrified vehicles are classified mainly by the degree of electrification, that is, by how much of the propulsion energy and power is electric, and by the energy source. Electric Vehicle System Engineering 1.1.4.1 B24EES502 Battery Electric Vehicles (BEV) A BEV stores all of its energy electrochemically and is propelled only by electric motors. It has no engine, fuel tank or exhaust. The battery is recharged from the grid through an on-board charger for AC supply or directly from an off-board DC fast charger, and partly by regenerative braking. Its strengths are the highest well-to-wheel efficiency of the four families when the electricity is low-carbon, mechanical simplicity and quiet operation. Its limitations are the mass and cost of the battery and the charging time, because range scales almost linearly with installed energy. Sections 1.2 and 1.7 examine its architecture and sizing. 1.1.4.2 Hybrid Electric Vehicles (HEV) An HEV combines an internal combustion engine (ICE) and at least one electric machine, and has no external charging. All net energy comes from fuel; the small battery only shifts energy in time. The hybrid gains efficiency in four ways: it stops the engine at idle, recovers braking energy, downsizes the engine, and runs it nearer its efficient operating region. Hybrids are also graded by the electric machine’s contribution. In a micro hybrid an uprated starter-generator provides stop-start. In a mild hybrid, often 48 V, the machine assists the engine but cannot normally propel the car alone. A full hybrid can drive short distances on electric power alone. 1.1.4.3 Plug-in Hybrid Electric Vehicles (PHEV) A PHEV is a hybrid whose larger battery can be charged from the grid. It normally starts in charge-depleting mode, using grid energy, and changes to charge-sustaining mode, behaving like an HEV, when the battery reaches its lower SoC limit. A PHEV can cover most daily trips electrically and still have the range of a fuel vehicle, at the price of carrying two complete energy systems. Its real-world benefit depends strongly on how regularly it is charged. A range-extended EV is effectively a series PHEV whose engine only drives a generator. 1.1.4.4 Fuel Cell Electric Vehicles (FCEV) An FCEV generates electricity on board in a fuel cell, normally a proton-exchange-membrane stack, by combining stored hydrogen with oxygen from air; the only exhaust product is water vapour. Traction is entirely electric, so its drivetrain resembles a BEV with the battery replaced by a stack and hydrogen tank plus a small buffer battery. Its advantages are fast refuelling and a high energy-to-mass ratio, which suits long-haul duty. Its limitations are sparse refuelling infrastructure, stack cost and durability, and the energy lost in producing, compressing and reconverting hydrogen. 1.1.5 Advantages and Limitations of EVs The advantages and limitations below apply principally to BEVs and should be read as engineering trade-offs, not as absolutes. Advantages.  13

• High tank-to-wheel efficiency and energy recovery during braking. • Zero tailpipe emissions, and low noise and vibration. • Full torque from standstill, with a wide constant-power speed range and a simple singlespeed reduction. • Fewer moving parts and no engine oil, clutch or exhaust after-treatment, which reduces routine maintenance. • Low centre of gravity, because the battery sits in the floor, and improved packaging freedom. • Precise and fast torque control, which benefits traction and stability control. Limitations. • The specific energy of batteries is far below that of liquid fuels, which increases vehicle mass for long range. • High initial cost, dominated by the battery pack. • Charging takes longer than refuelling, and charging infrastructure is unevenly distributed. • Range falls in very hot or cold weather because of cabin conditioning and cell behaviour. • Batteries degrade over time, and raw-material supply and end-of-life recycling need managing. • High-voltage safety, thermal-runaway protection and electromagnetic compatibility need careful design. 1.1.6 Comparison of Conventional ICE Vehicles and Electric Vehicles Table 1.2 compares the two vehicle concepts from an engineering perspective. Two contrasts deserve attention. First, the motor’s torque-speed curve already matches the traction demand, so a multi-speed gearbox is usually unnecessary (Fig. 1.10). Second, the comparison of energy stores is reversed by efficiency: although petrol stores roughly fifty times as much energy per kilogram as a cell, a BEV uses each kilowatt-hour about three times as effectively, so the net penalty in pack mass is smaller than the raw figures suggest. 1.1.7 Major Components of an Electric Vehicle Every EV is built from a small set of functional subsystems, listed in Table 1.3. Together they form three interacting domains: the electrical domain carrying power, the mechanical domain delivering torque to the road, and the control domain coordinating them. Electric Vehicle System Engineering 1.2 B24EES502 Configuration of Electric Vehicles The configuration of a vehicle describes how its energy sources, converters, machines and wheels are connected. The choice fixes which energy paths exist, and therefore which operating modes are possible, how large each component must be, and how the control problem is structured. Throughout this section electrical, mechanical and chemical paths use the colour convention given under the diagrams. 1.2.1 Basic Architecture of an Electric Vehicle Any EV can be regarded as three subsystems [1]. The electric propulsion subsystem comprises the vehicle controller, power converter, motor, mechanical transmission and driven wheels. The energy source subsystem comprises the source, its management system and the charging unit. The auxiliary subsystem comprises power steering, climate control and the low-voltage supply. Inputs from the accelerator and brake pedals are interpreted by the controller as torque demands, and the converter regulates the power flowing between source and motor. 1.2.2 Battery Electric Vehicle (BEV) Configuration Figure 1.2 shows the architecture of a typical single-motor BEV. The battery pack supplies DC power to the traction inverter, which converts it to controlled three-phase AC. The motor converts this into torque at speed ωm , and the reduction gear and differential scale it to the wheels. The double-headed arrows along the main chain mark the path as bidirectional, as energy reverses during regenerative braking. Electric Vehicle System Engineering 1.2.8 B24EES502 Single-Motor and Multi-Motor EV Architectures A single-motor architecture uses one machine with a differential (Fig. 1.7a,b). It is the lowestcost option and the efficiency map of a single machine is simple to manage. A multi-motor architecture uses two or more machines. Two axle motors (Fig. 1.7c) give AWD, redundancy and the chance to split torque so that both machines run efficiently. A motor at each driven wheel, or in-wheel motors (Fig. 1.7d), replaces the mechanical differential with an electronic one and allows torque vectoring, in which unequal left and right torque helps steer the car. Multi-motor systems raise component count and cost and need robust fault management, because an unbalanced torque is safety-critical. In-wheel machines also increase unsprung mass, which degrades ride quality, and they must survive the harsh wheel environment. 1.2.9 Powertrain Components and Their Functions Table 1.3 lists the functions of each component; here their interaction is considered. In motoring, the inverter imposes a voltage on the motor that produces the demanded torque; the gear reduces speed and multiplies torque; and the differential lets the wheels turn at different speeds in corners. Motor and inverter ratings are coupled by voltage and current: the back-EMF of the motor must stay below what the inverter can produce from the DC bus, and the phase current sets torque. The BMS and thermal system bound everything by supplying the allowable power of the battery and the temperature limits of the drive. 1.2.10 Mechanical and Electrical Power Transmission Paths The two power paths are described by different pairs of variables whose products give power: Pelec,DC = Vdc Idc , Pelec,AC = √ 3 VLL IL cos φ, Pmech = T ω, (1.5) where Vdc (V) and Idc (A) are the DC-bus voltage and current, VLL (V) and IL (A) are the rms line voltage and current, cos φ is the power factor, T (N m) is torque and ω (rad/s) is rotational speed. Electrical transmission allows flexible routing through cables and fast control, but demands high voltage to keep currents and I 2 R loss small. Mechanical transmission is highly efficient and compact over short distances but constrains the layout. Section 1.3.14 quantifies the recoverable energy. 1.3 Performance of Electric Vehicles The performance of a vehicle is what the driver experiences as acceleration, top speed, hillclimbing ability and range. All of these follow from one equation, Newton’s second law applied along the road. This section derives that equation term by term, then uses it to find the torque, power and energy that the powertrain must deliver. 1.3.1 Vehicle Performance Characteristics Vehicle performance is normally specified by the following measures. • Acceleration time, usually from 0 to 100 km/h. • Maximum speed, on a level road and sustained. • Gradeability, the steepest slope the vehicle can climb at a given speed. • Driving range, the distance on one charge under a stated cycle. • Energy consumption, in Wh/km, which is the EV counterpart of fuel consumption. The first three are power and torque requirements; the last two are energy requirements. This separation is important in design: motor and inverter follow from the former, and the battery energy from the latter.  22

The tyre deforms as it enters the contact patch and recovers as it leaves, but recovers less energy than was put in. Consequently the normal pressure is greater in the leading half of the patch, so the resultant ground reaction lies ahead of the axle and creates a moment opposing rotation. This moment is equivalent to a retarding force proportional to the normal load: Fr = Crr m g cos θ, (1.8) where Crr (dimensionless) is the rolling resistance coefficient, g = 9.81 m/s2 is gravitational acceleration, and θ (rad) is the road angle. For a passenger car on asphalt Crr is about 0.008–  23

0.015, and low-rolling-resistance EV tyres lie at the lower end. It rises with speed, tyre underinflation and rough surfaces. On slopes up to about 10% cos θ ≈ 1, so Fr is almost constant and depends mainly on mass. It dominates at low speed. 1.3.4 Aerodynamic Drag Resistance A moving vehicle transfers momentum to the air. Consider air of density ρ (kg/m3 ) approaching at relative speed v. The dynamic pressure is 12 ρv2 , so a body of frontal area A (m2 ) experiences a force proportional to 21 ρv2 A. A dimensionless drag coefficient Cd , which includes pressure drag due to flow separation and skin friction, makes this exact: Fa = 12 ρ Cd A (v + vw )2 , (1.9) where vw (m/s) is the headwind speed (zero in still air). At sea level ρ ≈ 1.225 kg/m3 . Typical modern EV values are Cd ≈ 0.22–0.32 and A ≈ 2.0–2.6 m2 . The quadratic dependence is decisive. Aerodynamic power grows with the cube of speed, Pa = Fa v, so doubling speed needs eight times the aerodynamic power. For this reason highway range is much shorter than urban range in EVs, the reverse of the usual ICE pattern, and why EV designers pursue low Cd A. 1.3.5 Gradient Resistance On a slope the weight mg resolves into a component normal to the road and a component along it. It identifies the largest losses, shows which component improvements offer the largest gain, and connects the vehicle to the wider energy system. It rests on one principle, the first law of thermodynamics: at every component, input power equals output power plus loss. Pin = Pout + Ploss , 1.4.1 η= Pout . Pin (1.29) Energy Flow in Battery Electric Vehicles Energy in a BEV flows along a single chain, but in both directions. In motoring, energy flows from battery to wheels and each component adds a loss. In regenerative braking, the chain reverses and the same components are traversed in the opposite order, so losses are incurred twice for any energy that is stored and reused. In addition, the auxiliary branch draws power continuously, regardless of whether the vehicle is moving. 1.4.2 Battery-to-Wheel Energy Conversion Figure 1.11 is the energy flow diagram during motoring. Electric Vehicle System Engineering 1.4.5 B24EES502 Energy Losses in Different EV Components Each component loses energy through distinct physical mechanisms, summarised below. • Battery. Ohmic and polarisation losses, modelled as Ploss ≈ I 2 Rint , where Rint (Ω) is the pack internal resistance. Losses rise with the square of current and at low temperature. • Inverter. Conduction loss, proportional to current through the device on-state drop, and switching loss, proportional to switching frequency. Section 1.8.17 gives expressions. • Motor. Copper loss 3I 2 R s in the stator, iron loss from hysteresis and eddy currents (rising with frequency), and mechanical friction and windage. • Transmission. Gear-mesh friction, bearing friction and oil churning. • Auxiliaries. Heating and air-conditioning can draw several kilowatts, which is often comparable to the traction demand in slow traffic. 1.4.6 Regenerative Braking Energy Flow Figure 1.12 shows the reverse flow. Electric Vehicle System Engineering 1.5.9 B24EES502 State of Health (SoH) State of health measures ageing relative to a new cell. It may be defined on capacity or on resistance: REoL − Rnow Qnow × 100%, SoHR = × 100%, (1.40) SoHQ = Qnew REoL − Rnew where REoL (Ω) is the resistance defining end of life. A traction battery is conventionally at end of life when capacity falls to about 80% of the initial value. Capacity fade cuts range; resistance growth cuts power and raises heat. 1.5.10 Depth of Discharge (DoD) Depth of discharge is the fraction removed from the fully charged state, DoD = 1 − SoC for a single discharge from full. Designers also use a usable window, for example 5–95% SoC, so that the BMS never exposes the extremes, which cause the most stress. Shallower average cycling greatly improves life, and so a pack sized with a margin may outlast the vehicle. 1.5.11 Cycle Life and Calendar Life Cycle life is the number of charge–discharge cycles before end of life under specified conditions; it depends on DoD, C-rate and temperature. Calendar life is the ageing that occurs with time alone, mainly by growth of the solid-electrolyte interphase on the anode. Calendar ageing accelerates with temperature and with high state of charge, so storing a vehicle at high SoC in heat is harmful. A useful sizing estimate links cycle life and lifetime distance: Dlife ≈ Ncyc R , (1.41) where Ncyc is the number of full-equivalent cycles and R (km) the usable range per cycle. For example, 1500 cycles at 300 km corresponds to 450 000 km. 1.5.12 Charging and Discharging Characteristics Figure 1.15 shows illustrative curves. On the left, cell voltage falls with discharged capacity. NMC falls smoothly from about 4.2 V, whereas LFP stays nearly flat near 3.3 V before dropping steeply at each end. Higher current displaces the curve down, because of the voltage drop across internal resistance: vt = OCV(SoC) − i Rint , (1.42) where vt (V) is the terminal voltage and OCV is the open-circuit voltage. The drop also ends discharge earlier at high rates, reducing usable capacity. The right of the figure shows the standard charging protocol. In the constant-current (CC) phase, the voltage rises to the upper limit; in the constant-voltage (CV) phase, the charger holds that limit and current tapers as the cell approaches full. The CV taper is why fast charging is usually quoted as 10–80%, and why the last 20% takes disproportionately long. Charge rate is further restricted at low temperature, when lithium plating on the anode would damage the cell.  38

The anode is commonly graphite, sometimes with silicon added, on a copper foil. The cathode is a lithium metal oxide or phosphate on an aluminium foil. A porous separator keeps the electrodes apart while the organic liquid electrolyte conducts ions. During discharge, lithium ions leave the anode and intercalate into the cathode, while electrons travel through the external circuit and deliver power. Charging reverses the process. For a layered-oxide cathode, the reactions on discharge are Anode: Cathode: Li x C6 → C6 + x Li+ + x e− , − Li1−x MO2 + x Li + x e + → LiMO2 , (1.44) (1.45) where M denotes transition metals such as Ni, Mn, Co or Al. The cell voltage is the difference between the electrochemical potentials of the two electrodes, so the cathode chemistry defines most of the voltage and capacity [14]. 1.5.16 LFP, NMC, NCA and LTO Battery Technologies The dominant technologies differ mainly in their cathode, except for LTO, which replaces the graphite anode. Figure 1.17 shows a distributed architecture. Slave boards attached to each module measure cell voltages and temperatures and perform cell balancing. They communicate over an isolated link with a master controller. The master also reads pack current, runs estimation and fault logic, and controls the contactors and pre-charge. It reports allowable charge and discharge power to the VCU and charger over CAN, and requests cooling or heating from the thermal loop. The main functions are the following. 1. Measurement: cell voltage, pack current, temperature, insulation resistance. 2. Estimation: SoC, SoH and state of power. 3. Protection: over-voltage, under-voltage, over-current, over-temperature and isolation faults, by derating or by opening contactors.  41

Too cold, and resistance rises and fast charging risks lithium plating. Too hot, and ageing accelerates and, past the onset temperature, thermal runaway may start. The heat generated in a pack is approximately Q̇gen ≈ I 2 Rint , (1.46) and the lumped thermal balance is Mc p dT = Q̇gen − hA s (T − T c ) , dt (1.47) where Q̇gen (W) is the heat generation, M (kg) the pack mass, c p (J/kg K) the specific heat, T (K) the pack temperature, h (W/m2 K) the heat transfer coefficient, A s (m2 ) the cooled surface area and T c (K) the coolant temperature. Equation (1.47) shows two design levers, thermal mass and the hA s product. Air cooling has a low h and is confined to smaller or low-power packs; liquid cooling through cold plates or channels is the standard for cars; immersion cooling offers still better performance and is emerging for fast-charging applications. Heaters or heat pumps warm the pack in cold climates. 1.5.19 Battery Selection Considerations for EV Applications Battery selection follows the duty. The principal considerations are as follows. • Energy requirement: range target and vehicle consumption (Eq. (1.22)).  42

• Power requirement: the peak discharge and charge power expressed as C-rate. • Voltage: set by the motor and inverter design and by fast-charging needs. • Life: daily distance, climate, and warranty target. • Safety and regulation: chemistry stability and homologation requirements. • Packaging and mass: available floor area and height. • Cost and supply: cell price and material availability. A simple rule is that the power-to-energy ratio (in h−1 , numerically a C-rate) identifies the class of cell needed. A long-range car with 100 kW and 60 kWh needs only 1.7C, so a high-energy cell suffices. A small hybrid with 30 kW and 1.5 kWh needs 20C, so it needs a high-power cell. In Indian conditions, high ambient temperature and cost sensitivity favour LFP for electric three-wheelers, buses and mass-market cars, whereas NMC remains common where range per kilogram matters most. 1.6 Drive Cycle and Its Importance in System Analysis 1.6.1 Definition of a Drive Cycle A drive cycle is a standardised or measured record of vehicle speed against time, v(t), that represents a type of driving. It defines the accelerations, cruises, decelerations and stops that a vehicle must follow. A regulatory cycle is performed on a chassis dynamometer under controlled conditions so that vehicles can be compared on an equal basis. Sometimes the term also includes a road gradient profile, θ(t), but the standard chassis cycles assume a level road. 1.6.2 Importance of Drive Cycles in EV Design Section 1.3 gave instantaneous equations; a drive cycle provides the time history that turns them into design figures. It is used in the following ways. • Regulation and labelling: energy consumption and range are homologated on a stated cycle. • Component sizing: peak and root-mean-square torque and power fix motor and inverter ratings, and cycle energy fixes the battery. • Efficiency evaluation: operating-point distribution over a motor map predicts average efficiency. • Thermal and durability design: current profiles drive thermal models and battery ageing tests.  43

• Control development: energy management and regeneration strategies are compared over identical conditions, for example in NREL’s ADVISOR or MathWorks Powertrain Blockset [17, 30]. No regulatory cycle exactly represents real driving; the choice of cycle changes the declared range, so the same car has different ranges under MIDC, WLTC and EPA tests. Quoted range should always be read together with its cycle. 1.6.3 Speed-Time Representation of Drive Cycles A drive cycle is a sampled time series, usually at 1 Hz, plotted as speed against time. Figure 1.18 shows the illustrative cycle used in this unit, constructed for teaching and clearly not an official test cycle. Its upper trace has low-speed urban trips, then a suburban section and a short high-speed portion. The lower trace is wheel power for the reference vehicle, computed with Eq. (1.13). Comparing the two is instructive. Power spikes occur in acceleration phases, and are highest when accelerating at high speed; cruising needs only a modest plateau that grows with speed; braking gives negative power that is available for regeneration. Electric Vehicle System Engineering 1.6.4.1 B24EES502 Indian Driving Cycle (IDC) The IDC is a short modal cycle for two- and three-wheelers in India, based on observed lowspeed traffic. It comprises six repeats of a 108 s cycle, giving 648 s and about 3.9 km at an average of about 21.9 km/h, with a peak speed of about 42 km/h [20]. It is widely quoted for electric scooters, so its low speed gives ranges well above what a rider would obtain on faster roads. 1.6.4.2 Modified Indian Driving Cycle (MIDC) The MIDC is the Indian cycle for passenger cars, with a structure like NEDC: four repetitions of a 195 s urban section followed by a 400 s extra-urban section. The total duration is 1180 s and the distance about 10.7 km. The extra-urban maximum speed is 90 km/h [21], a limit that differs from NEDC. Because it is gentle, MIDC ranges are generally optimistic compared with WLTC ranges for the same car. 1.6.4.3 New European Driving Cycle (NEDC) NEDC is a modal cycle, used in Europe until replaced by WLTP from 2017, and comprises four repeats of the urban ECE-15 section and one extra-urban EUDC section. It lasts 1180 s and covers about 11 km, with a 120 km/h peak and a mean speed of about 34 km/h. Figure 1.19 gives a simplified illustration of this urban-plus-extra-urban structure. Its smooth, constantacceleration segments are not representative of real driving, which was the principal reason for replacing it. Electric Vehicle System Engineering 1.7.19 B24EES502 Regenerative Braking Considerations Regenerative braking influences sizing in three respects. The motor and inverter are normally symmetric in torque, but the battery’s charge limit is usually smaller than its discharge limit, so charge acceptance often sets the maximum regen power. Thus at high SoC or low temperature regeneration may be cut sharply. The friction brake system must still handle a full stop without regeneration. And brake blending must respect tyre adhesion distribution and stability; the front axle takes more brake force, which is a reason that RWD vehicles cannot regenerate all braking. 1.7.20 Safety Margins and Design Constraints Beyond performance, the design must satisfy the following constraints. • Thermal limits of motor windings, magnets, semiconductor junctions and cells. • Tyre adhesion limit, Eq. The inverter chosen here now becomes the subject of the following sections. 1.8 Three-Phase Inverter 1.8.1 Introduction to Power Inverters An inverter is a power-electronic converter that converts DC power into AC power with controllable voltage, frequency and phase. It works by switching semiconductor devices on and off rapidly, so that the output is a sequence of voltage pulses whose average over a short interval follows the desired waveform. Devices operate as near-ideal switches, either fully on or fully  58

off, which keeps the loss small even at high power: a switch ideally has either zero voltage or zero current, and so dissipates no power [4]. 1.8.2 Role of Inverters in EV Powertrains The traction inverter sits between the DC battery and the AC motor (Fig. 1.2). It performs four functions. 1. It produces the variable-frequency, variable-voltage supply that sets motor speed and torque. 2. It carries out the fast current control that makes torque response nearly instantaneous. 3. It reverses power flow for regenerative braking, with no extra hardware, because each switch has an antiparallel diode. 4. It protects the machine and battery against over-current, over-voltage and overtemperature. Its efficiency directly enters Eq. (1.26), and it must withstand high current, automotive vibration and coolant temperatures. Silicon IGBTs have long been the norm at 400 V, and SiC MOSFETs are spreading quickly because their lower switching loss suits higher voltage and higher frequency. 1.8.3 Classification of Inverters Inverters are classified according to several attributes. • By number of output phases: single-phase, three-phase, or multiphase. • By source type: voltage source (VSI) or current source (CSI). • By number of output levels: two-level, or multilevel such as neutral-point-clamped. • By control method: six-step (square wave) or pulse-width modulated. • By commutation: hard-switched or soft-switched (resonant). 1.8.4 Single-Phase and Three-Phase Inverters A single-phase full-bridge has two legs, and its output alternates across one load. Instantaneous single-phase power pulsates at twice the output frequency. A balanced three-phase system instead delivers constant instantaneous power, p(t) = va ia + vb ib + vc ic = 3Vrms Irms cos φ, (1.65) where v x and i x are the instantaneous phase voltages and currents. Equation (1.65) is the reason three-phase machines produce smooth torque and are universal in EV traction, with singlephase inverters confined to low-power uses such as portable loads or vehicle-to-load outlets.  59

Electric Vehicle System Engineering 1.8.5 B24EES502 Voltage Source Inverter (VSI) A VSI is fed from a stiff DC voltage, usually a battery in parallel with a low-impedance capacitor. Its output voltage waveform is set by the switching pattern, while its output current depends on the load. All traction inverters are of this type, because a battery is naturally a voltage source. The DC-link capacitor supplies the high-frequency current pulses drawn by the switching bridge, so that the battery and its cables see a smooth current. A leg must never have both switches on: that would short-circuit the DC link, an event called shoot-through. 1.8.6 Current Source Inverter (CSI) A CSI is fed from a stiff DC current, obtained by placing a large inductor in series with the source. Its switches steer this current through the phases, so that its output current waveform is defined and the voltage depends on the load. Its switches must block reverse voltage, and it has inherent short-circuit robustness. However, the large DC inductor is heavy and lossy, and the regulation of current needs an additional front-end stage. Table 1.13 summarises the comparison, and it shows why the VSI dominates in EVs. The next three sections consider the most important question left open here, namely how the switches are to be driven. 1.9 PWM Techniques 1.9.1 Introduction to Pulse Width Modulation Pulse width modulation (PWM) controls the average output over a short period by varying the fraction of time for which a switch is on. If a leg’s upper switch is on for time ton in a period T s , the mean pole voltage is 1 v̄aO = Ts ∫︂ T s 0 (︂ )︂ vaO dt = Vdc d − 12 , d= ton , Ts (1.80) where d (dimensionless) is the duty ratio. Letting d vary slowly and sinusoidally yields a sinusoidal average voltage. The high-frequency pulses are then filtered by the motor’s inductance, so the current is nearly sinusoidal. The principle is known as the volt-second balance: over each switching period, the pulses must deliver the same volt-seconds as the desired waveform. 1.9.2 Importance of PWM in EV Motor Drives PWM is what allows the fixed battery voltage to become a smooth, adjustable AC supply. It matters in EV drives for these reasons. • Amplitude and frequency of the output are controlled independently, which allows fast torque and flux control. • Low-order harmonics are eliminated and distortion is moved near the switching frequency, reducing torque ripple and loss. • Fast response is obtained, since the voltage is updated every carrier period. • It is available from any automotive microcontroller via dedicated timer peripherals. 1.9.3 Switching Frequency The switching frequency f s = 1/T s (Hz) is the rate at which a leg’s devices switch, set in carrier PWM by the carrier frequency, so f s = fc . It trades ripple against loss, Eq. (1.79). It also influences audible noise: values within the human hearing band, up to 10 kHz or so, can be objectionable, especially in quiet EVs. Control bandwidth is limited to a small fraction of f s , usually by a factor of about 10.  67

Diagonal switch pairs are driven together, so the output swings between +Vdc and −Vdc . Harmonics appear around fc . • Unipolar PWM. Electric Vehicle System Engineering 1.9.14 B24EES502 Advantages and Limitations of SPWM Advantages. • Simple to implement, with one comparison per leg and low processor load. • Linear voltage gain up to ma = 1. • Fixed switching frequency and a predictable harmonic spectrum. Limitations. • Only 78.5% of the six-step fundamental is available in the linear range. • Each phase is treated independently, so the three-phase structure of the load is not exploited. • More switching and more current ripple than optimised sequences at the same frequency for high modulation indices. • Non-linear overmodulation behaviour. The bus limitation can be overcome by adding a common-mode (zero-sequence) offset to all references. Because the motor neutral is isolated, such an offset leaves line voltages unchanged. Third-harmonic injection and the min-max offset are examples [10], and the latter is the carrierbased equivalent of SVPWM. 1.10 Space Vector Pulse Width Modulation (SVPWM) 1.10.1 Introduction to Space Vector Representation Rather than modulating each phase independently, SVPWM treats the inverter and motor as a single three-phase system [9]. It represents the three phase voltages by one rotating vector and synthesises it from the eight states of Table 1.14. This viewpoint is natural for AC machines, because the three stator currents produce a single rotating magnetic field, whose direction and magnitude are what really matter. It also fits field-oriented control, which outputs a voltage vector, and gains a higher DC-bus utilisation than SPWM. 1.10.2 Three-Phase Voltage Space Vector The three windings of a machine are spaced 120◦ apart in space. In the example drive of Example 6, the extra 15% voltage increases the speed at which field weakening starts, lowers the current needed at top speed, and maintains torque at low SoC. Discontinuous variants, used at high modulation, reduce inverter loss, and overmodulation up to six-step is used in the field-weakening range, where bus utilisation is at a premium. Reference [5] gives an extensive treatment of these drive applications. 1.11 Hysteresis Current Control 1.11.1 Introduction to Hysteresis Current Control PWM methods generate a voltage and rely on an outer loop to regulate current. Motor torque depends on current, so an alternative is to control the current directly. Hysteresis current control (HCC), or bang-bang control, does this with no modulator at all: it compares the measured phase current with its reference and switches the leg whenever the error leaves a tolerance band [11]. It has the fastest possible response for a given inverter, since it acts on each error as it occurs. Its drawback, examined below, is a variable switching frequency. 1.11.2 Operating Principle Consider phase a of Fig. 1.21. With S 1 on, a positive voltage across the winding drives current up; with S 4 on, a negative voltage drives it down. The controller holds the current within a band around the reference by choosing between these two states. It behaves in the same way as a thermostat, which allows the room temperature to wander within limits. Figure 1.31 shows the mechanism over a few switching cycles. 1.11.3 Reference Current and Actual Current The reference current i∗x (t) for each phase comes from the torque controller, usually as a sinusoid that is synchronised with rotor position: i∗a = Iˆ sin ωt, )︂ (︂ , i∗b = Iˆ sin ωt − 2π 3 (︂ )︂ i∗c = Iˆ sin ωt + 2π , 3 (1.113) where Iˆ (A) is set by the torque demand and ω (rad/s) by rotor speed. The actual current i x (A) is measured with Hall-effect sensors or shunts, usually at high bandwidth. The tracking error is e x (t) = i∗x (t) − i x (t).  (1.114) 82

With an isolated neutral, the three currents sum to zero, so only two are independent. Therefore each leg’s switching changes the neutral potential and disturbs the other two phases. Limitations. • Variable switching frequency, with a spread harmonic spectrum and acoustic noise. • Switching loss cannot be fixed, making thermal design more conservative. • Interaction among phases for an isolated neutral. • Digital implementation needs very high sampling rates: a loop at fsample overshoots the band, by up to T sample di/dt. • Higher ripple at low speed for a given band, and poor low-current behaviour near zero crossings. 1.11.11 Applications in Electric Vehicle Motor Drives HCC is well-suited to drives in which torque response and simplicity matter more than harmonic quality. It has been used for switched-reluctance traction motors, in which phase current profiling is natural, and for low-cost brushless DC drives in light electric vehicles. In mainstream PMSM cars, fixed-frequency FOC with SVPWM is preferred, for reasons of NVH and EMC, but HCC concepts remain as a fast peak-current limit. Direct torque control is a related method, which applies hysteresis to torque and flux rather than to currents [5]. 1.11.12 Comparison with Carrier-Based PWM and SVPWM HCC differs from the previous two methods in one basic respect: SPWM and SVPWM are voltage modulators with a fixed period, inside a current loop; HCC is itself the current loop, with no fixed period. So carrier methods offer predictable spectra and losses, but response is limited by sampling and PI bandwidth. HCC reverses that trade-off. The complete comparison follows in Section 1.12. 1.12 Comparison of PWM Techniques The three techniques of Sections 1.9–1.11 can now be compared directly. At low speed and high torque, back-EMF is small and modulation index is small, so voltage headroom is irrelevant, whereas current ripple and audible noise matter because little road or wind noise masks them. Continuous SVPWM at a fixed frequency is therefore preferred. SVPWM and SPWM behave similarly at this point. In urban and highway cruise, the drive runs at part load for most of its life. Loss reduction determines the range, so discontinuous SVPWM is attractive at moderate to high modulation, where the clamped leg reduces switching loss. At high speed in the field-weakening region, the inverter runs out of voltage. SVPWM’s extra 15% is valuable, and overmodulation towards six-step gives the highest torque per ampere at the top of the speed range, at the expense of low-order harmonics. As m f falls, synchronisation of the switching pattern with the fundamental is needed. In fast transients and faults, the hysteresis principle retains its value. Even in drives using SVPWM, a hardware comparator commonly limits peak current on a cycle-by-cycle basis, because it responds in microseconds, without waiting for the next sampling instant. For cost-sensitive auxiliaries such as coolant pumps and small compressors, SPWM’s simplicity is an advantage, and bus utilisation is less important. For switched-reluctance or trapezoidal BLDC drives, the required current pulses suit hysteresis control, which is preferred. For the 100 kW traction drive of Example 6, the appropriate choice is therefore field-oriented control with SVPWM at a fixed 10 kHz, using discontinuous modulation at higher modulation indices, overmodulation at top speed, and a hardware hysteresis comparator for peak-current protection.  91

Unit 2: EV Traction Batteries, Battery Management Systems and Charging Systems The traction battery is the largest, heaviest and most expensive component of a battery electric vehicle (BEV). Its energy sets the range, its power sets the acceleration and regenerative capability, its voltage sets the architecture of the inverter and charger, and its ageing sets the service life of the vehicle. This unit develops the subject in the order an engineer meets it: selecting a storage technology, understanding how a cell works, sizing a pack, estimating its internal states, modelling it, managing it through a battery management system (BMS), and finally charging it. Notation and sign convention. Throughout this unit the battery current I is taken as positive during discharge and negative during charge. State of charge is written as z (or SoC) and is dimensionless, 0 ≤ z ≤ 1. Capacity Q is quoted in ampere-hours (Ah); wherever it appears with time in seconds it is converted to coulombs using 1 Ah = 3600 C. Specific quantities are per kilogram and density quantities are per litre. 2.1 Ragone Plot 2.1.1 Introduction to the Ragone Plot Every energy storage device must answer two independent questions: how much energy can it hold, and how fast can that energy be delivered? A single number cannot answer both. The Ragone plot, named after D. V. Ragone, who used it in 1968 to compare battery systems for electrically powered vehicles [1], answers both at once by plotting the specific power of a device against its specific energy on logarithmic axes. Its theoretical basis was later formalised by Christen and Carlen [2]. 2.1.2 Definition and Significance A Ragone plot is a log–log chart with specific energy on one axis and specific power on the other. Each storage technology occupies a region, not a point, because a real device delivers less energy when it is discharged at higher power. The chart is significant because a single glance shows whether a technology can meet a vehicle’s energy requirement and power requirement with an acceptable mass, and how long a discharge can be sustained.  12

The latter are called energy density and power density: ev = E , V pv = P , V (2.4) where V is the volume in litres. A passenger-car floor pack is usually volume-limited, because the underfloor space is fixed, whereas a two-wheeler or an aircraft is more sensitive to mass. The terms are often loosely interchanged, so a careful engineer always checks the units. Values must also be compared at the same level (cell, module or pack), because housing, cooling and busbars typically reduce the cell-level specific energy by 25–40% at pack level. 2.1.5 Interpretation of the Axes Figure 2.1 shows a Ragone plot with specific energy on the horizontal axis and specific power on the vertical axis. Both axes span several decades, which is the reason for the logarithmic scale: a supercapacitor and a fuel-cell system differ by more than two orders of magnitude in each coordinate. Moving right means more energy (more range); moving up means more power. Devices in the upper left deliver bursts lasting seconds, whereas devices in the lower  13

right sustain low power for hours. They remain suitable for 12 V auxiliary service and for low-cost light vehicles. • Nickel-metal hydride (NiMH) batteries roughly double the lead-acid energy and were the workhorse of early hybrid vehicles. • Lithium-ion batteries span a wide region. Energy-optimised cells reach the right of the chart; power-optimised cells trade energy for power and move upward and left. • Supercapacitors store charge electrostatically. They have very high specific power and cycle life but very little energy, so they discharge within seconds. • Fuel-cell systems are energy converters with an external fuel tank. Their energy depends on the mass of stored hydrogen and is therefore high, but their power per kilogram is moderate, so they sit at the lower right. Fuel-cell vehicles normally need a battery buffer. Figure 2.2 isolates the specific energy axis so that the technologies can be ranked directly. Note the factor of about ten between lead-acid and lithium-ion at the top of its range, and the further factor of about ten between lead-acid and a supercapacitor. This single comparison explains why long-range BEVs became practical only with lithium-ion cells.  14

Representative values compiled from [3, 4]; individual products differ. 2.1.7 Battery and Supercapacitor Performance Characteristics A battery stores energy in chemical bonds, so charge must cross an interface and diffuse through solids. These are slow, thermally activated steps, which limit power. A supercapacitor stores energy in the electric double layer, with no bulk chemical reaction, so its power is limited chiefly by its low series resistance. Its stored energy is E = 12 CV 2 , which falls with the square of the voltage; consequently a supercapacitor bank needs a DC-DC converter to use its energy fully. It also has a high self-discharge rate compared with a lithium-ion battery. 2.1.8 Trade-off between Energy and Power Density The curve of a real device bends downward at high power because internal losses grow with current. This can be derived from the simple Voc –R model. Let a cell with open-circuit voltage Voc , resistance R and capacity Q deliver a constant power P to a load. The terminal voltage Vt = Voc − IR and P = Vt I give 2 RI − Voc I + P = 0 ⇒ I= Voc − √︁ 2 − 4RP Voc , 2R (2.5) the smaller root being the stable operating point. The discharge lasts t = Q/I, so the delivered energy is 2RPQ E(P) = Pt = . (2.6) √︁ 2 − 4RP Voc − Voc As P → 0, E → QVoc , the full stored energy. A real solution exists only when P ≤ Pmax = 2 Voc /(4R), which is the maximum power transfer condition; at that point half the energy is lost inside the cell. Equation (2.6) is precisely the knee of the Ragone curve. The physical origin of the trade-off lies in electrode design, as illustrated in Fig. 2.3. A highenergy cell uses thick electrodes to pack in more active material, but ions must then travel a longer path, which raises resistance. A high-power cell uses many thin electrode layers with a large interfacial area and short ion paths, but more of its mass is inactive foil and separator.  15

Its limitations should be stated explicitly: • It says nothing about cost, cycle life, calendar life, safety or charging capability.  17

• Published regions mix cell, module and system-level data; comparing them directly is misleading. • The curve assumes constant-power discharge at one temperature, whereas a vehicle sees a dynamic profile over a wide temperature range. • The curves shift with state of charge and ageing, as Section 2.5 shows. • It ignores volume unless a separate volumetric chart is drawn. • It ignores charge acceptance. Regenerative braking and fast charging are limited by different mechanisms from discharge. 2.2 Battery Types and Battery Pack 2.2.1 Introduction to Electrochemical Batteries An electrochemical battery converts chemical energy directly into electrical energy through spatially separated oxidation and reduction reactions. Strictly, a cell is the basic electrochemical unit and a battery is a connected group of cells, although common usage calls either a battery. 2.2.2 Primary and Secondary Batteries Primary batteries are designed for a single discharge because their reactions are not practically reversible. Secondary batteries can be recharged many times because the reaction can be reversed by an external current. Traction batteries are always secondary. Figure 2.4 classifies the technologies considered here. Primary (non-rechargeable) Alkaline, zinc–carbon, lithium metal Lead-acid Electrochemical batteries Aqueous electrolyte Secondary (rechargeable) Nickel-cadmium Nickel-metal hydride Non-aqueous or solid electrolyte Lithium-ion Lithium-polymer Sodium-ion Solid-state Figure 2.4: Classification of battery technologies by rechargeability and electrolyte family. The first branch in Fig. 2.4 separates single-use from rechargeable cells. The second branch reflects an engineering boundary: water decomposes at about 1.23 V (thermodynamically),  18

which limits aqueous cells to roughly 2 V, whereas organic and solid electrolytes allow 3–4 V cells. Because energy scales with voltage, this is the main reason why non-aqueous systems lead in specific energy. 2.2.3 Classification of Rechargeable Batteries The following subsections review each rechargeable family in terms of its construction, reactions, nominal voltage, strengths and limitations [3]. 2.2.3.1 Lead-Acid Batteries A lead-acid cell has a lead dioxide positive plate, a sponge lead negative plate and a sulphuric acid electrolyte. On discharge both plates convert to lead sulphate: Pb + PbO2 + 2H2 SO4 discharge ⇌ charge 2PbSO4 + 2H2 O, Vnom ≈ 2.0 V. (2.8) The technology is low in cost and highly recyclable, and it has high surge capability for its cost, which suits engine starting. However, it has low specific energy, poor deep-cycle life, and suffers sulphation if left discharged. It survives in EVs mainly as the 12 V auxiliary battery and in low-speed vehicles. 2.2.3.2 Nickel-Cadmium Batteries A NiCd cell uses nickel oxyhydroxide and cadmium in an alkaline potassium hydroxide electrolyte, with a nominal voltage of 1.2 V. It is robust, tolerates abuse and works at low temperatures, but cadmium is toxic and the cell shows the memory effect. Its use in vehicles has been effectively abandoned, largely for environmental reasons. 2.2.3.3 Nickel-Metal Hydride Batteries NiMH replaces cadmium with a hydrogen-absorbing metal alloy. It keeps the 1.2 V nominal voltage but offers higher capacity and better environmental acceptability. It was used widely in hybrid vehicles due to its long shallow-cycle life and tolerance of overcharge. Its drawbacks are high self-discharge, a low coulombic efficiency at high SoC, and heat generation at the end of charge. 2.2.3.4 Lithium-Ion Batteries Lithium-ion cells shuttle lithium ions between two host materials (Section 2.4). With a nominal voltage of about 3.2–3.7 V for graphite-based cells, they lead in specific energy and offer high coulombic efficiency and long cycle life. They need a BMS for safe operation because they tolerate no overcharge and can enter thermal runaway. 2.2.3.5 Lithium-Polymer Batteries The term “lithium-polymer” is used loosely. Commercial cells so described are normally lithium-ion cells with a gelled polymer electrolyte or simply a pouch format. The chemistry  19

is otherwise the same; the benefit is packaging flexibility and low mass. Genuine solid polymer electrolyte cells, which usually run at elevated temperature, are a different and much rarer technology. 2.2.3.6 Sodium-Ion Batteries Sodium-ion cells follow the same rocking-chair principle, replacing lithium with sodium. Sodium is abundant and the cathode can avoid nickel and cobalt, and aluminium can replace copper as the negative collector. Hard carbon replaces graphite since sodium does not intercalate into graphite adequately. Specific energy is currently below that of LFP, although the cells show good low-temperature performance, so they are attractive for low-cost, shorter-range vehicles and stationary storage [5]. 2.2.3.7 Solid-State Batteries Solid-state batteries replace the flammable liquid electrolyte with a solid ionic conductor (sulphide, oxide or polymer), which may enable a lithium metal negative electrode and therefore higher specific energy. Open challenges include interfacial resistance, dendrite growth, stack pressure and manufacturing scale [6]. They should be treated as an emerging technology; claimed values for pre-commercial cells are not comparable with mass-production data. 2.2.4 Comparison of Battery Technologies Table 2.1 collects the main characteristics. Electric Vehicle System Engineering 2.2.7.3 B24EES502 Thermal Management Provisions Cell ageing and safety depend strongly on temperature, so packs normally have cold plates, a coolant loop and sometimes a heater. Air cooling suits only low-power small packs, while liquid cooling is the norm for passenger-car packs. The aim is both a target mean temperature, typically 20–40◦ C, and a low temperature spread across cells, typically a few degrees. 2.2.7.4 High-Voltage Battery Safety Components These include main positive and negative contactors, a pre-charge circuit, a fuse or pyrotechnic disconnect, the MSD, the current sensor, an insulation monitor, a high-voltage interlock loop (HVIL), and vent paths. Their operation is explained in Section 2.13. 2.3 Basic Battery Operation 2.3.1 Electrochemical Energy Conversion A cell produces electricity because the two electrode materials have different electrochemical potentials. When an external circuit is closed, a spontaneous reaction proceeds, but it is divided into two half-reactions at separate electrodes. Electrons cannot travel through the electrolyte, so they are forced around the external circuit to do work, whereas the ions complete the circuit inside the cell. 2.3.2 Construction: Electrodes, Electrolyte, Separator and Collectors Figure 2.11 shows the universal structure of a cell. • The anode is the electrode where oxidation occurs and the cathode the one where reduction occurs. These labels strictly interchange during charge, so in rechargeable cells it is safest to speak of the negative and positive electrodes. By industry convention, “anode” means the negative electrode and “cathode” the positive, named for discharge. • The electrolyte is an ionic conductor and electronic insulator. • The separator is a porous, electronically insulating membrane that prevents electrode contact while letting ions pass. • The current collectors are metal foils that carry electrons between the electrode material and the terminals. 2.3.3 Electrochemical Potential Each electrode has an electrode potential that reflects the free energy of its reaction. Using lithium metal directly proved unsafe due to dendrites, so the lithium-ion cell instead keeps lithium in ionic form within host materials [7, 8]. 2.4.2 Working Principle, Intercalation and Deintercalation A lithium-ion cell is a “rocking-chair” device: lithium ions shuttle between two hosts and no bulk metal plating occurs in normal operation. Intercalation is the reversible insertion of ions into a host lattice; deintercalation is their extraction. Figure 2.16 shows the concept: the graphite layers keep their structure while lithium enters and leaves the gaps between them. For LFP the positive reaction is FePO4 + Li+ + e− → LiFePO4 . The charge is carried by the working lithium ion; the amount of cyclable lithium is therefore a key inventory which decreases with ageing. 2.4.5 Lithium-Ion Transport Ion transport comprises solid diffusion in the active particles, charge transfer at the particle surface, and migration and diffusion in the electrolyte. At high rates, the electrolyte becomes depleted near the positive electrode on discharge, and at low temperatures diffusion slows dramatically. These limits explain the falling capacity at high C-rate and low temperature. 2.4.6 SEI Layer and its Importance During the first charge, the electrolyte reduces on the graphite surface at low potential, forming the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) [10]. A good SEI passes Li+ but blocks electrons and solvent, stopping further electrolyte decomposition, so it is essential for stability. Its formation consumes some cyclable lithium, which is the origin of the first-cycle capacity loss. Over life the SEI thickens slowly, which is the main mechanism of calendar ageing and resistance growth [11]. 2.4.7 Cell Voltage and Operating Voltage Range Voltage limits are chemistry-specific. NMC/graphite cells commonly operate between about 2.5–3.0 V and 4.2 V with a nominal around 3.6–3.7 V, whereas LFP/graphite operates about 2.5–3.65 V with a very flat 3.2–3.3 V plateau. Exceeding Vmax degrades the cathode and electrolyte, and discharging beneath Vmin can dissolve the copper collector. Figure 2.19 compares representative curves. The flat LFP plateau gives steady power but makes voltage-based SoC estimation difficult, a point revisited in Section 2.7. 2.4.8 Capacity, Specific Energy and Specific Power Practical capacity depends on the active material loading, the voltage window, the rate and the temperature. Note that a 1C discharge ideally lasts one hour regardless of cell size. High charge rates give convenience, but they raise heat and risk lithium plating. 2.4.12 Lithium Plating On charge, the graphite potential falls. If it reaches that of metallic lithium, Li+ deposits as metal on the particle surface instead of intercalating [12]. This occurs at high charge rate, at low temperature, or at high SoC. Plating consumes cyclable lithium, can grow dendrites  33

through the separator, and is the main reason fast charging is restricted at low temperature and tapered at high SoC. 2.4.13 Thermal Runaway Fundamentals Thermal runaway is a self-accelerating exothermic failure [13]. Triggers include mechanical damage, an internal short, overcharge or external heating. As temperature rises, a sequence follows: the SEI decomposes, the anode reacts with electrolyte, the separator melts allowing an internal short, the cathode releases oxygen, and the electrolyte burns. Each stage feeds the next because heat generation grows exponentially with temperature (Arrhenius behaviour), whereas heat rejection grows only about linearly. The danger at pack level is propagation between cells. Hence the BMS must detect the early signs and the pack must be designed to delay propagation. 2.4.14 Important Lithium-Ion Chemistries Lithium iron phosphate (LFP). LiFePO4 cathode, graphite anode, nominal 3.2 V. The strong P–O bond resists oxygen release, giving excellent thermal stability, long cycle life and low cost, with no cobalt or nickel. Its drawbacks are a lower specific energy and voltage, a flat OCV, and poor low-temperature performance. It is used widely in buses, entry-level cars and, increasingly, mainstream cars. Lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide (NMC). LiNi x Mny Coz O2 , graphite anode, nominal 3.6–3.7 V. The ratio is denoted NMC111, NMC622, NMC811 by proportion; more nickel gives higher capacity but less thermal stability, and less cobalt reduces cost. It is the mainstream of long-range BEVs. Lithium nickel cobalt aluminium oxide (NCA). LiNi0.8 Co0.15 Al0.05 O2 -type cathode, nominal about 3.6 V. Offers very high specific energy, but it needs careful thermal control, and is less tolerant of abuse. Lithium cobalt oxide (LCO). LiCoO2 , nominal about 3.7 V. It has high volumetric energy density but cobalt-related cost and limited thermal stability, so it is used in consumer electronics rather than traction. Lithium titanate (LTO). Li4 Ti5 O12 anode with NMC or LMO cathode, nominal about 2.3– 2.4 V. The anode operates at about 1.55 V versus Li, which avoids plating and SEI growth, so it has very long life and high charge rates, even in the cold. Its low voltage gives low specific energy and high cost per kWh, restricting it to specialised buses and high-cycle applications. Other emerging chemistries. These include lithium manganese iron phosphate (LMFP), which raises the LFP voltage; silicon-rich anodes; lithium-rich and high-manganese cath-  34

odes; and lithium-sulphur, which offers high theoretical specific energy but a short life so far. Sodium-ion and solid-state cells were covered in Section 2.2. EKF assumes a sufficiently accurate model, approximately Gaussian noise, and small linearisation error. It corrects initial errors and provides an error bound. On the other hand it requires tuning of Q and Rv and more computation, and its accuracy depends on the model parameters, which vary with temperature and age. 2.7.1.8 Unscented Kalman Filter Rather than linearising, the UKF propagates a small set of deterministically chosen sigma points through the true nonlinear functions, and recovers the mean and covariance from them. It needs no Jacobians and copes better with strong nonlinearity, at the cost of more function evaluations per step. 2.7.1.9 Adaptive Estimation Techniques Adaptive filters update the noise covariances or the model parameters online. Examples include adaptive EKF, dual EKF (one filter for states, another for parameters), and fusion with recursive least squares. They mitigate the parameter drift with ageing, but they increase the risk of instability, and need careful design. 2.7.1.10 Machine Learning-Based SoC Estimation Data-driven methods learn the map from measured voltage, current and temperature to SoC, using neural networks such as feed-forward or long short-term memory networks, or support vector regression. They need no explicit electrochemical model, but require large, representative training data, generalise poorly outside it, and are harder to certify for safety. Hybrids that combine a learned model with a physics-based filter are an active research area [19]. 2.7.1.11 Effect of Temperature and Ageing; Initial SoC and Sensor Errors Temperature changes OCV slightly, and changes capacity and resistance significantly, so model parameters must be scheduled on temperature. Ageing reduces Qn ; if the SoC calculation keeps using the new-cell value, the gauge will read high. Initial SoC uncertainty arises from long rest with self-discharge and from the hysteresis of OCV, and it is corrected by a closed-loop estimator. Sensor errors have three forms: current offset, which causes drift by (2.52); gain  50

In EV engineering, models serve four purposes: vehicle-level simulation of range and performance; design of the BMS estimators of Section 2.7; pack design, including thermal and balancing studies; and virtual testing of control software in MATLAB/Simulink before hardware exists [24]. 2.11.2 Electrochemical Models versus Equivalent Circuit Models Electrochemical models, such as the Doyle–Fuller–Newman model, solve coupled partial differential equations for concentration and potential. They reveal internal states such as the anode potential, which is valuable for plating-free fast charging, but they require many hard-tomeasure parameters and heavy computation. Equivalent circuit models (ECMs) instead reproduce the terminal behaviour using a voltage source, resistors and capacitors [25, 26]. ECMs have few parameters and can run on a BMS processor, so they dominate on-board use. Their drawback is that the parameters are empirical and vary with SoC, temperature and age. 2.11.3 Ideal Voltage Source Model The simplest representation, shown in Fig. 2.44, is Vt = Voc . Each element has a physical interpretation: • Open-circuit voltage source Voc (z): the equilibrium voltage. Its dependence on z makes the model behave like a very large capacitor. • Ohmic resistance R0 : electrolyte, foil, tab and contact resistance, responsible for the instantaneous step. • Polarisation resistance R1 : the voltage drop from charge transfer and diffusion, once settled. • Polarisation capacitance C1 : sets how quickly that drop develops, with τ1 = R1C1 . The transient voltage response is governed by these time constants, and the steady-state response is reached after about 5τ, when the capacitor current has decayed to zero, and V1 = IR1 . Thereafter only OCV drifts. Together these yield the dynamic battery behaviour.  69

Since every cell must remain inside its voltage limits, the pack stops charging when the first cell reaches Vmax , and stops discharging when the first reaches Vmin . Cell balancing is the process of equalising the cells so that the pack can use its full capacity. 2.12.2 Cell Voltage Imbalance, Capacity Imbalance and their Causes Voltage imbalance denotes a spread of terminal voltages, which, at rest, reflects a spread in SoC. Capacity imbalance is a spread in the Ah capacity itself. The causes include: • manufacturing tolerance in capacity, resistance and self-discharge; • temperature gradients across the pack, since warmer cells age and self-discharge faster; • unequal ageing and mismatch that grows over the service life; • parasitic loads of monitoring electronics that differ between modules.  78

It is simple, but voltage under load includes IR differences, and on flat curves the voltage hardly reveals SoC, so it is normally done at rest or at the top of charge. SoC-based balancing equalises the estimated SoC and can run at any time, so it works better for LFP, but it depends on the estimator. Capacity-aware methods go further by accounting for each cell’s capacity using (2.109). 2.12.6.2 Balancing Thresholds, Current, Losses and Efficiency The algorithm needs an on-threshold, an off-threshold to prevent chatter, a temperature guard, and an accurate voltage measurement: thresholds are usually around 5–20 mV, and depend on the AFE accuracy and chemistry. The balancing charge is proportional to current and time, so a large pack with low balancing current may need many hours. Overvoltage and undervoltage protection act on the worst cell. Overcurrent and short-circuit protection have different speeds: an overcurrent limit is managed by software through limits, but a short circuit far exceeds what a contactor can reliably break, so a fuse or pyrotechnic device clears it. Over- and undertemperature protection consider that charge limits are stricter than discharge limits. Thermal runaway detection. Because cell temperature is not measured everywhere, modern packs fuse several clues: rapid temperature rise, sudden voltage drop, pack pressure and gas sensors. The aim is to warn occupants early. Insulation monitoring. The high-voltage bus floats with respect to the chassis, so a single insulation fault is not immediately dangerous, but a second would be. An insulation monitor measures the resistance between each rail and chassis. UN Regulation No. 100 sets minimum values relative to working voltage, namely 100 Ω/V for DC circuits and 500 Ω/V for AC circuits in its usual form [28], while the Indian AIS-038 is aligned with this regulation [29]. 2.13.8 Communication Interfaces and CAN Controller Area Network (CAN) is the usual link between BMS and the vehicle. It is a differential two-wire, multi-master bus with message priority and error detection. Classic CAN typically runs at up to 500 kbit/s on such buses, while CAN FD permits larger, faster payloads. Between AFEs, the common choices are isolated daisy chains and, increasingly, wireless links. 2.13.9 BMS Interaction with EV Control Systems Figure 2.67 shows the network. The vehicle control unit (VCU) requests a drive or charge mode. The BMS answers with SoC, power limits and fault status. The inverter respects the current limits when converting the driver’s torque request. During charging, the BMS talks to the on-board charger, or through the charge controller to a DC station, and requests target voltage and current. The thermal system receives coolant requests. 2.13.10 Battery Safety and Fault Diagnosis Fault diagnosis must distinguish a genuine hazard from a sensor fault. The flowchart of Fig. 2.68 shows how: each check has a debounce time, and faults are classed by severity. A warning leads to derating and a diagnostic trouble code; a critical fault leads to contactor opening. BMS software is normally developed in line with the functional-safety approach of ISO 26262. Unit 2 (continued): Battery Chargers and Charging Systems The energy that the battery delivers must be returned safely, efficiently and conveniently. Charging joins three systems that are designed by different parties: the grid, the charging equipment and the vehicle. Their interaction is governed by power electronics, control, communication and regulation, in that order of this chapter. 3.1 Basic Requirements for Charging Systems 3.1.1 Introduction and Purpose of EV Battery Chargers A charger converts electrical power from the supply to the controlled DC voltage and current demanded by the battery. Its purposes are to restore energy in the required time, without harming the battery or the grid, and to protect the user. Note a matter of terminology: the equipment on the wall, the electric vehicle supply equipment (EVSE), is a charger only in the DC case. In AC charging, the EVSE merely delivers protected AC power, while the actual converter is in the vehicle. 3.1.2 Basic Charging Requirements • Charging power, voltage and current. The charger must span the whole battery voltage window at the required current, P = Vb Ib . Both output limits matter: for a fixed current limit, a low-voltage pack charges at a lower power. • Charging efficiency. This is the fraction of grid energy that reaches the battery, including AC-DC and DC-DC stages: ηchg = Ebat /Egrid . • Charging time. From (3.13) below, time is set by energy and power, and, for chemistry reasons, by tapering at high SoC. • Battery chemistry compatibility. Voltage limits and permitted rates are chemistryspecific, and the charger follows the BMS request. • Charging safety and isolation. Grid and battery must be isolated in most designs by a high-frequency transformer, so that a single fault cannot put the chassis at a dangerous potential. • Power factor. The charger must draw near-sinusoidal current in phase with the voltage, which requires an active power factor correction stage.  90

• Harmonic distortion. Rectifier currents contain harmonics, which load the distribution system, so total harmonic distortion must be kept low. For the current, it is defined by THDI = √︂∑︁ ∞ 2 h=2 Ih I1 (3.1) , where Ih is the rms value of harmonic h and I1 the fundamental. The true power factor is then cos φ1 PF = √︂ . (3.2) 2 1 + THDI • Bidirectional charging. A charger with a reversible power stage can return energy, which is treated in Section 3.2.3.4. • Communication between EV and station. Both parties must agree on limits, start and stop. • Battery temperature monitoring. The BMS reports cell temperature, and the charging current is reduced accordingly, or cooling is applied. • Overvoltage and overcurrent protection. These apply on both AC and DC sides, independent of the control loop. • Environmental conditions. Enclosures must withstand heat, rain, dust, and voltage fluctuation. Batteries must be preheated in cold conditions or precooled for fast charging in high ambient temperature. 3.1.3 Onboard and Offboard Charging Systems Figure 3.1 shows the overall charging architecture and the essential distinction. An onboard charger (OBC) travels in the vehicle, so its power is limited by mass, cost and cooling, and it uses AC from an EVSE. An offboard charger remains at the station, where mass and cooling are not as restricted, so it can feed DC at high power directly to the battery, bypassing the OBC. pilot / PLC Vehicle AC EVSE (protection, pilot) AC On-board DC Battery charger + BMS AC grid DC EVSE (AC/DC + DC/DC) DC ISO 15118 / CAN Figure 3.1: EV charging architecture: AC path through the onboard charger, DC path from an offboard charger.  91

The filter limits conducted emissions into the grid and protects against surges. • Rectifier and power factor correction (PFC). A rectifier and boost stage shape the input current to follow the voltage, and regulate a DC link. • DC-DC conversion and isolation. Electric Vehicle System Engineering 3.2.1.2 B24EES502 Single-Phase, Three-Phase and Bidirectional OBCs Single-phase OBCs serve domestic connections and are commonly around 3.3 kW or 7.4 kW. The input power pulsates at twice line frequency, so the DC link needs a large capacitor. Threephase OBCs, typically 11 kW or 22 kW, use a three-phase PFC stage and have a smoother power flow. Bidirectional OBCs replace diodes with active switches, typically using a totempole PFC and DAB, so power can flow from the battery to the AC side. 3.2.2 Offboard Charger An offboard or DC charger, shown in Fig. 3.4, takes three-phase AC from a low-voltage or medium-voltage connection and converts it in two stages: an active front-end rectifier with PFC, then isolated DC-DC modules. For high-power charging, several modules are paralleled, and connections from the MV level may use a dedicated transformer. The charging cable and connector are often liquid-cooled at the highest currents, to keep the cable manageable. On the battery-side interface, the DC is connected straight to the pack through vehicle-side contactors. The charger controller exchanges limits with the BMS and, separately, connects to a back-end for authorisation and billing. It is efficient and simple, and it is the worldwide norm. 3.2.3.2 Wireless Charging: Static and Dynamic Wireless (inductive) charging transfers power between a ground coil and a vehicle coil through a resonant, high-frequency magnetic field. Compensation capacitors tune the coils so that a modest coupling across an air gap can transfer power. Static charging operates in a parking bay and offers convenience. Dynamic charging supplies power to a moving vehicle via coils embedded in the road, which might reduce the battery size, but it has high infrastructure cost and is still at the pilot stage. Efficiency depends strongly on alignment.  93

Electric Vehicle System Engineering 3.2.3.3 B24EES502 Battery Swapping In battery swapping, a discharged pack is replaced by a charged one in minutes. It separates charging from the vehicle’s parked time, and is attractive for two- and three-wheeler fleets in India. Packs may be charged off-peak. It needs standard packs, a stock of extra batteries, and a business model for ownership. IS 17896 addresses swap systems [30]. 3.2.3.4 Bidirectional Charging: V2G, V2H, V2L and V2B Bidirectional charging treats the vehicle battery as a distributed energy resource: • Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G): energy is exported to the grid under aggregator or utility control, for peak support or frequency services. • Vehicle-to-Home (V2H): the vehicle supplies a household, usually in a backup role, or to shift solar energy. • Vehicle-to-Building (V2B): the principle of V2H is scaled for a commercial building, chiefly to shave peak demand. • Vehicle-to-Load (V2L): the vehicle offers an AC socket to power tools or appliances. The cost of V2G is the extra cycling of the battery, and the need for grid-code compliance, anti-islanding and metering, together with the high-level communication of ISO 15118-20 [31]. The result is independent of battery size, because the current is in C-rate. 3.3.5 Trickle Charging, Multi-Stage and Pulse Charging Trickle charging. A small continuous current compensates for self-discharge. It suits leadacid and NiMH float service. It is not used in the usual sense for lithium-ion cells, because they cannot absorb overcharge; however, a small current is used to recover deeply discharged cells to the safe voltage, which is often called pre-charge or trickle. Multi-stage charging. A series of decreasing constant currents, sometimes called multi-stage constant current, is used, with each stage ending at a voltage limit. It approximates the battery’s permissible current, with a higher rate at low SoC where plating risk is low. Pulse charging. Current is applied in pulses separated by rests or brief discharges, aiming to allow concentration gradients to relax. Reported benefits vary [32], so it should be seen as an option to verify experimentally for each cell. 3.3.6 Fast Charging and Opportunity Charging Fast charging at rates of about 1–3C or more is limited by lithium plating, heat, and the power available. Modern protocols use a stored map of allowed current against SoC and temperature [32]. Opportunity charging is a short top-up whenever the vehicle stops, such as a bus at a terminal. It keeps the battery at partial SoC, and permits a smaller pack, which suits LFP and LTO chemistries.  100

In Mode 3, the EVSE tells the vehicle its limit through the control pilot, and the OBC must not exceed it. IEC 61851-1 defines charging modes as summarised in Table 3.3 [33]. 3.4.1.2 DC Charging Current and Voltage–Current Operating Limits In DC charging, the station and vehicle exchange their maximum voltage, current and power, and the vehicle requests a current inside the overlap. The EVSE follows [34]. Its operating envelope has a constant-current boundary (limited by the cable and module current), a constantpower boundary (limited by supply), and a maximum voltage boundary. A 400 V car at a 500 A, 1000 V station is therefore limited to about 200 kW by its own voltage, and a station’s nameplate figure is not the same as the power delivered.  102

Thus the rating in an IEC configuration is a maximum, while a product may be rated lower.
