The specific configurations are covered in Section 3.5. 3.4.3 Electrical Protection 3.4.3.1 Overcurrent Protection Every charging point needs a dedicated final circuit with its own overcurrent device. The design load must be taken as continuous, as a charging session runs at full current for hours, and a diversity factor of unity generally applies unless an automatic load management system is installed [36, 37]. 3.4.3.2 Residual Current Protection A person’s safety relies upon residual current devices (RCDs). In a charger, the rectifier can produce smooth DC fault currents, which can blind a conventional Type AC or Type A RCD by saturating its core. IEC 60364-7-722 therefore requires protection for each connection point by an RCD with a rated residual current of not more than 30 mA, of at least Type A, with additional measures against DC fault currents [38]. Measures commonly used are a Type B RCD, or a Type A RCD together with a residual direct current detecting device (RDC-DD) to IEC 62955 [39], which disconnects the supply on DC fault current. For Mode 2, IEC 62752 covers the IC-CPD [40]. In India, the National Electrical Code 2023 follows a similar approach [36], as summarised in [37]. 3.4.3.3 Earthing, Grounding and Isolation Monitoring The protective conductor bonds the vehicle body to the installation earth, and its continuity is continuously verified via the control pilot circuit. Indian practice refers to IS 3043 for earthing and IS 732 for wiring [37]. In isolated DC systems, an insulation monitoring device (IMD)  103

checks the DC bus before and during a session, as required by IEC 61851-23 [34]. Further, the DC coupler must be locked before energising, and it must stay locked while the voltage is above a safe limit. 3.4.4 Power Quality, Power Factor, Harmonics and Grid Connection Large charging loads are non-linear, and they appear suddenly, which matters to the distribution company. In India, the requirements for connection flow from the CEA (Technical Standards for Connectivity) regulations and from the licensee’s supply code, and they refer to harmonic limits of the IEEE 519 kind [41]. The Ministry of Power guidelines describe the connection process, referred to in the next subsection. 3.4.5 Communication, Safety and Charging Infrastructure Requirements A compliant installation must provide, among other things: fire-retardant enclosures with suitable IP rating; a cable length limit; surge protection; mechanical protection from vehicles; emergency stop; and periodic inspection. Public chargers must also be networked to permit interoperable roaming through open protocols. 3.4.6 Indian Regulatory Framework 3.4.6.1 Ministry of Power Guidelines The Ministry of Power issued the Guidelines for Installation and Operation of Electric Vehicle Charging Infrastructure–2024 in September 2024 [42], with an amendment on 10 January 2025 [43]. Public summaries report the following provisions [44]: • Setting up a charging station is a de-licensed activity. • A single-part tariff is specified: not more than the average cost of supply (ACoS) until 31 March 2028, with 0.7 times ACoS in solar hours (9:00 to 16:00) and 1.3 times ACoS in other hours. • Ceilings are set for service charges, which differ for AC and DC charging and the time of day. The notified tables should be consulted. • Connection timelines for a new connection are 3 days in metropolitan areas, 7 days in other municipal areas, 15 days in rural areas, 30 days in rural hilly terrain, and 90 days where a line extension or substation is needed. • Separate metering is required. • The density targets for 2030 are reported as one station within a 1 km grid in urban areas and every 20 km along highways, with long-range points every 100 km for buses and trucks [45].  104

The 2025 amendment refines the definitions of charging infrastructure and of a charging station, supports round-the-clock operation, requires technology-agnostic land allotment bids, and revises the nodal agency provision [43]. The EVSE drives a ±12 V signal through 1 kΩ. Resistors in the vehicle pull the positive level down, and the EVSE reads the result to know the state: state A at +12 V for no vehicle; state B at +9 V for connected; state C at +6 V for ready to charge (with S2 closed); state D at +3 V for ventilation required; state E at 0 V for error; and state F at −12 V for EVSE fault. OCPP 1.6 and 2.0.1 are widely deployed, and OCPP 2.1 has been published as IEC 63584210:2025 [55]. OCPI is a separate protocol for roaming among networks. 3.5.3.5 EV–EVSE Communication, Authorisation, Plug and Charge, and Smart Charging A DC session proceeds through a handshake: connection, compatibility check (limits), isolation test, pre-charge, energy transfer under the vehicle’s current requests, and shut-down. Unit 3: Introduction to Power Electronics and Electric Drive Train Systems An electric vehicle is, electrically, a chain of energy conversions: the grid supplies alternating current, the battery stores direct current, and the traction machine needs variable-frequency, variable-voltage alternating current. Power electronics connects these three worlds, and the electric drive turns the result into controlled mechanical motion. This unit therefore moves from converters (Sections 3.1 and 3.2), through the drive train and its mechanics (Sections 3.3 to 3.6), to the two dominant traction machines, the induction motor (Sections 3.7 to 3.11) and the permanent magnet synchronous machine (Sections 3.12 to 3.16). Electric Vehicle System Engineering 3.1.1 B24EES502 Introduction to Power Electronics Power electronics is the efficient conversion and control of electrical power using semiconductor switches. A switch is ideally either fully on, with no voltage across it, or fully off, with no current through it, so it dissipates no power in either state. Output voltage is then controlled not by dropping voltage across a resistive element, but by the fraction of time the switch is on. Inductors and capacitors, which also store energy without dissipation, smooth the chopped waveform. This is why conversion efficiencies of 95–99% are routinely achieved at tens of kilowatts [1–3]. 3.1.2 Importance of Power Electronic Converters in Electric Vehicles Converters decide much of what a driver experiences: acceleration comes from fast torque control, range depends on conversion losses, and charging time depends on charger power [4,5]. Every watt lost in an inverter must also be removed by the cooling system. In summary, the converters must • supply the machine with variable voltage and frequency from a fixed-chemistry DC source whose voltage varies with state of charge; • permit energy to flow in reverse during braking; • interface the vehicle to the grid at near-unity power factor; • feed the low-voltage electrical system, the compressor and the heater from the highvoltage battery. 3.1.3 Power Electronic Conversion Stages in EVs Figure 3.1 shows the complete power electronics architecture of a battery electric vehicle (BEV). The high-voltage battery is the central node. The traction path, drawn horizontally, runs through an optional bidirectional DC-DC converter and the traction inverter to the motorgenerator, and every arrow on it is double-headed because braking reverses the flow. Around this path sit three supporting converters: the on-board charger, the off-board fast charger connection, and the isolated DC-DC converter for the 12 V network. Auxiliary inverters drive the air-conditioning compressor and similar loads. Figure 3.2 arranges the same stages in the order of energy flow in a BEV. During AC charging, energy passes through rectification with power factor correction and then through an isolated DC-DC stage into the battery. During driving, it passes through the traction stage to the wheels. Note that the battery divides the system into a charging side that is often unidirectional and a traction side that must be bidirectional. A hybrid electric vehicle (HEV) adds a second source. In the power-split arrangement of Figure 3.3, the engine drives a generator MG1, whose AC output is rectified by Inverter 1 on to a shared DC bus. Inverter 2 feeds the traction machine MG2. Electric Vehicle System Engineering 3.1.4.3 B24EES502 DC-AC Converters An inverter synthesises AC from DC. The traction inverter is the largest example. 3.1.4.4 DC-AC-DC Conversion Isolation is not possible at DC, because a transformer needs changing flux. An isolated DC-DC converter therefore inverts the DC to high-frequency AC, passes it through a small transformer, and rectifies it again. Since transformer size falls as frequency rises, this DC-AC-DC structure is far smaller than a line-frequency transformer of the same rating. 3.1.4.5 Unidirectional and Bidirectional Converters A unidirectional converter passes power one way and can use diodes in place of some switches, which is simpler and cheaper. A bidirectional converter uses active switches in every position, so current can reverse. Traction stages must be bidirectional, and chargers are increasingly so. 3.1.4.6 Isolated and Non-Isolated Converters A non-isolated converter has a conductive path between input and output, and is small and efficient. An isolated converter has a transformer, which provides safety separation and a large voltage ratio, at some cost in size and loss. Table 3.2 compares the converters used in an EV. Fast and resistive, used at low voltage up to about 150 V, for example in 48 V systems. • Silicon IGBT. Bipolar conduction gives a low drop at 600–1200 V and high current. Tail current limits switching frequency to around 10–20 kHz. IGBTs have been the mainstream traction device. • SiC MOSFET. Silicon carbide has a wide bandgap and roughly ten times the critical field of silicon, so 1200 V devices have low on-resistance and switch quickly [8]. Lower losses, especially at part load, and higher temperature capability make SiC the favoured device for 800 V platforms, though at higher cost. • GaN HEMT. Very fast and well-suited to on-board chargers and DC-DC converters at about 650 V. 3.1.11 Gate Driver Circuits A gate driver turns a logic-level signal into the gate voltage and charge the device needs. For a MOSFET or IGBT, the driver charges the gate capacitance through a resistor, which sets di/dt and dv/dt. Upper-leg drivers need isolated supplies and isolated signal paths, because the source of the upper device swings at the full link voltage. Drivers also provide dead-time insertion, desaturation (short-circuit) detection, soft turn-off, undervoltage lockout and, for SiC, a negative turn-off voltage that resists false turn-on. 3.1.12 DC-Link Capacitor The DC-link capacitor supplies the pulsed inverter current, keeps the link stiff and absorbs regenerative transients. Its current rating, not its capacitance, is usually the design constraint: for a two-level VSI the rms capacitor ripple current is of the order of half the load phase rms current at the worst-case modulation [6]. A simple sizing rule follows from the charge supplied in a period, C ≥ Iripple /(2π f s ∆V) as an approximation. Film capacitors are preferred over  27

electrolytics for their long life, high ripple rating and low inductance. The link’s parasitic inductance must be small, since it causes voltage overshoot when devices switch off. 3.1.13 Thermal Management of Power Converters Heat flows from the semiconductor junction through a chain of thermal resistances to the coolant, and the steady-state junction temperature is T j = T cool + Ploss Rth, jc . (3.18) Rth, jc (in K/W) here is the total junction-to-coolant value. Traction modules typically use direct liquid cooling through pin-fin baseplates, on a water-glycol loop that often shares a circuit with the motor. Temperature cycling fatigues bond wires and solder, so lifetime depends on the amplitude of temperature swings as well as their peak value. Control software estimates T j and derates current as limits are approached. 3.2 Electric Vehicle Charger Topologies 3.2.1 Introduction to EV Charger Topologies Unit 2 treated charging from the standpoint of the battery and its standards. It splits naturally into an electrical part and a mechanical part, joined at the motor. An EV drive train is much simpler than that of a conventional car, since a traction motor produces torque from zero speed over a wide speed range, so there is no clutch and usually only one gear ratio [15]. 3.3.2 EV Powertrain Architecture and Components Figure 3.32 shows the complete architecture. Heavy double arrows form the energy path, and dashed arrows are signals. The driver’s pedal request reaches the vehicle control unit, which  37

issues a torque command to the motor controller after considering limits from the battery management system. The components are: • Battery system. Stores energy and sets the DC voltage, as covered in Unit 2. • Power electronic converter. Controls voltage, current and frequency (Section 3.1). • Electric traction motor. Converts electrical to mechanical power and back. • Transmission system. A reduction gear trades speed for torque, so a small high-speed motor can provide high wheel torque. • Differential. Divides torque equally between wheels of an axle, while permitting different wheel speeds in a turn. • Drive shaft. Carries torque to the wheel hubs through constant-velocity joints. • Wheels and tyres. Convert torque to tractive force through the tyre-road contact. Adhesion, not motor torque, is often the limit. • Motor controller. Executes the fast current loops and generates inverter switching commands. • Vehicle control unit (VCU). Interprets driver demand, arbitrates limits, blends regenerative and friction braking and coordinates all subsystems. Maximum current produces high torque. Battery power rises with speed until the power limit is reached. • Cruising. Torque just balances road load. The motor often runs at part load, in which case efficiency depends on low iron and switching losses. • Deceleration. Lifting the pedal commands negative torque, so the vehicle coasts down under a mild regenerative load.  41

Each maps to the torque-speed envelope. Its rotor current is induced from the stator, which is why it is also called an asynchronous machine. As the cage is shortcircuited, currents flow and these interact with the field to give force on each bar. By Lenz’s law, the force acts to reduce the relative motion, so it drags the rotor along behind the field. If the rotor reached synchronous speed, the relative motion would vanish, as would the induced current and the torque; hence a motor always runs with some slip. Above synchronous speed, slip is negative, and the machine generates: this is how an induction machine regenerates. Torque is produced by the interaction of the field with the in-phase component of rotor current, T e = k Φm Ir cos φr , (3.55) where φr is the rotor power-factor angle and k a machine constant. Near zero slip, rotor current is proportional to slip and largely resistive, so torque rises linearly with slip. At large slip, rotor reactance dominates and torque falls. In an induction motor, one set of stator currents produces both flux and torque, so a sudden change in voltage disturbs both. Vector control, based on the principle of field orientation due to Blaschke [21], restores the DC-machine behaviour by viewing the stator current in a frame that rotates with the rotor flux. 3.9.2 Scalar Control Versus Vector Control The simplest IM drive is the open-loop inverter of Figure 3.65, in which a speed command sets frequency and a V/f profile sets voltage. Closed-loop scalar control, as in Figure 3.66, adds a slip regulator: the speed error gives a slip command, which is added to the measured speed  67

to give the stator frequency ω∗e , and the voltage follows from V = V0 + Kωe . The boost V0 compensates stator resistance drop at low speed. No rotor current is needed to establish flux, so there is almost no rotor copper loss, and the rotor turns at exactly synchronous speed. Electric Vehicle System Engineering 3.12.6 B24EES502 EV Traction Requirements, Advantages and Limitations Advantages: • High power density. Magnets supply flux at no cost in copper, so the machine is compact. • High efficiency. Rotor loss is small, and peak efficiency often reaches around 97%. • Regenerative braking. Back EMF is available at all speeds, so generation requires no magnetising power. • Good thermal path. Most losses are in the stator, near the cooling jacket. Limitations: • Thermal limitations. Remanence falls with temperature, by about 0.1%/K for NdFeB, which reduces torque. • Demagnetization. Excessive negative d-axis MMF at high temperature can permanently damage magnets. Control limits and thermal protection must prevent this. • Field weakening. The magnet flux cannot be turned off, so weakening requires continuous stator current. At high speed, an inverter fault can result in uncontrolled generation into the DC bus, because the back EMF can exceed the link voltage. • Cost and supply. Rare-earth prices and supply are a strategic concern. Tables 3.15 and 3.16 compare the machines. Electric Vehicle System Engineering 3.16.2 B24EES502 Principle of Rotor Flux Orientation The Park angle is θe = pθm + θ0 , where θ0 is a calibrated offset between the sensor and the magnet north axis. With this, the d axis lies on the magnet by construction, iq is the torque current, and id controls the net d-axis flux. Current decoupling then means that, in the rotor frame, the two currents can be set independently by separate loops. 3.16.3 Rotor Position Feedback Figure 3.117 shows the position chain. A resolver, a rotary transformer, gives sine and cosine signals modulated by an excitation carrier. It is robust against heat and vibration, and hence the automotive standard. A resolver-to-digital converter (RDC) or software tracking observer extracts angle and speed. An encoder gives higher resolution by digital pulses but is less tolerant of the environment. An angle error ∆θ rotates the frame, producing a torque error of about T e (1 − cos ∆θ) together with d-axis disturbance. Offset calibration is therefore a production step. For regeneration, i∗q < 0. By (3.137), torque changes sign, and the DC current reverses through the inverter diodes and switches, with no change of control structure. For an IPMSM in regeneration, MTPA keeps id < 0 and β moves into the third quadrant of the current plane, since reluctance torque follows the sign of id iq . A well-tuned PMSM drive gives a torque rise time of 1–2 ms, far quicker than the mechanical time constants of a vehicle, so the torque response is effectively instantaneous from the driver’s viewpoint. Performance is constrained not by the controller but by DC-link voltage (particularly at low state of charge), by thermal limits, and by torsional oscillation in the driveline, for which the rate limiter of Algorithm 19 and active damping are used. Unit 4: EV Modelling and Simulation 4.1 Introduction to EV Modelling and Simulation 4.1.1 Introduction to EV System Modelling An electric vehicle is a coupled system. Electrical energy leaves the battery, passes through an inverter and motor, turns into torque at the wheels and finally appears as motion, aerodynamic heat, tyre heat and a small amount of stored kinetic and potential energy. A change anywhere in this chain affects everything else. Heavier batteries add range but also add road load; a higher gear ratio improves launch torque but raises motor speed at cruise and may push the motor into a less efficient region. A model is a set of equations and data that captures these interactions, and a simulation is the numerical solution of that model for a chosen scenario [1, 2]. Units 2 and 3 described the battery, power converters and machines individually. This unit joins them into complete vehicle models, and uses those models to answer questions such as: how much energy does a car need on a test cycle, how much of the braking energy can be recovered, what size of motor and battery will meet a specification, and how far can the car travel? 4.1.2 Importance of EV Modelling and Simulation Prototype testing is slow and expensive, and a chassis dynamometer can only test hardware that already exists. Simulation is valuable for these reasons: • Cost and time. Thousands of battery, motor and gear combinations can be screened in the time it takes to build one prototype. • Early decisions. The most expensive choices, such as pack voltage, cell format and drive layout, are made before hardware exists. • Safe testing. Faults, thermal runaway precursors and extreme braking can be explored without risk to people or equipment. • Repeatability. A simulated test is exactly repeatable, so the effect of one parameter can be isolated. • Control development. Algorithms can be tested against a virtual vehicle before they are loaded on an ECU. 4.1.3 Objectives of EV Simulation A simulation study always starts with a stated objective, because that objective decides which model is adequate. Typical objectives are to predict energy consumption and range over a  15

drive cycle; to size the battery, motor and inverter; to evaluate acceleration, top speed and gradeability; to quantify regenerative energy recovery; to develop and tune control strategies; and to estimate component stresses such as peak current, temperature and duty. 4.1.4 Modelling Terms: Definitions and Differences Six terms are often confused. Their meanings are distinct, and Table 4.1 summarises them. 1. Mathematical modelling expresses system behaviour as equations, for example δmv̇ = Ft − Fres . It is an abstraction: the equations hold only under stated assumptions. 2. Physical modelling builds a model by connecting components that exchange energy, such as a battery connected to an inverter through electrical ports. The tool writes the equations from the topology. Simscape is a common example [34]. 3. Simulation is the numerical solution of a model over time for specified inputs and initial conditions. 4. System identification estimates model parameters from measured data, for example fitting R0 , R1 and C1 to a current pulse test (Unit 2) or fitting road-load coefficients to a coast-down test. 5. Model verification asks: did we solve the equations correctly? It checks code, units, solver accuracy and energy balance. 6. Model validation asks: did we build the right model? It compares predictions with independent measurements over the intended operating range. Table 4.1: Modelling terms and the question each answers Term Question answered Mathematical modelling Which equations describe it? Physical modelling How are components connected? Simulation What happens for this input? System identification What are the parameter values? Verification Is the model solved correctly? Validation Does it match reality? A perfectly verified model can still be invalid if an important loss was left out, and a model can match one test by accident while containing a coding error that cancels another error.  16

Reading across each row shows the act of idealisation: a pack containing hundreds of cells becomes a voltage source behind a resistance, a gear train becomes a ratio and an efficiency, and the whole vehicle body becomes a single point mass. These equations reappear throughout this unit. A model is static if its output depends only on the present input, for example a motor efficiency map. It is dynamic if it has memory, written as differential equations with state variables. In general form, (︁ )︁ (︁ )︁ ẋ(t) = f x(t), u(t), p , y(t) = g x(t), u(t), p , (4.1) where x is the state vector (vehicle speed v in m/s, state of charge z, polarisation voltage V1 in V and so on), u is the input vector, p is the parameter vector and y is the output vector. The states hold the system’s energy storage, which is why a model of an EV usually needs at least v (kinetic energy) and z (electrochemical energy). In a numerical solution, (4.1) is stepped forward with a solver. The simplest is forward Euler, xk+1 = xk + ∆t f(xk , uk , p), (4.2) with step ∆t in s. It is accurate and stable only if ∆t is small relative to the fastest time constant. 4.1.6 Simulation-Based Design and the Simulation Workflow Simulation-based design uses models as the main design tool, with hardware tests reserved for confirmation. Figure 4.2 shows the workflow. The objective is defined first, parameters are collected, the model is built and its code verified. It is then validated against data. A mismatch sends the work back to parameter identification, rather than forward to conclusions. MATLAB and Simulink are the most widespread for modelbased design [32]. Powertrain Blockset provides pre-built drive-cycle and vehicle reference models [33], Simscape Electrical provides physical network models, and Stateflow provides state machines. NREL’s ADVISOR was an early public vehicle simulator that popularised the combined backward/forward approach [11, 12], and NREL’s FASTSim is a fast open tool for energy and range studies [13]. Commercial platforms such as GT-SUITE, AVL Cruise and Altair tools provide integrated multi-physics environments. 4.1.13 Introduction to MATLAB and Simulink for EV Modelling MATLAB is a text-based numerical environment, suitable for parameter scripts, postprocessing and calculations over arrays of samples, as in a backward-looking model. Simulink is a graphical block-diagram environment, in which signals flow between blocks and a solver advances the states. It suits closed-loop dynamic models such as a forward-looking model. Electric Vehicle System Engineering 4.1.14 B24EES502 Integrated EV Simulation Platforms An integrated platform connects several domains in one environment: electrical, mechanical, thermal and control. Its value lies in capturing cross-coupling, such as a hot battery reducing the power limit, which in turn slows the car, which in turn changes the energy used. Trade-offs between mass, drag and rolling resistance can be expressed in Wh/km. • Battery sizing. The cycle consumption and range target fix usable energy; peak power fixes C-rate (Sections 4.9 and 4.11). • Motor selection. Operating points on the torque-speed plane show which machine suits the duty (Section 4.11). • Inverter selection. Peak and rms current follow from torque demand and voltage. • Energy consumption prediction. This is the main output of a drive-cycle simulation (Section 4.3). • Range estimation. Consumption and usable energy together give range (Section 4.15). • Regenerative braking analysis. Simulation shows how much braking energy reaches the battery after limits and losses (Section 4.6). • Control strategy development. Controllers are tuned against a virtual vehicle (Sections 4.7 and 4.13). • Performance optimisation. Parameters are swept, or optimised, against a cost such as lifetime energy cost. 4.1.16 Reference Vehicle Used in This Unit For consistency, all simulations and most worked examples use the hypothetical reference BEV of Table 4.3. A driver sees a target speed and moves the pedals. The pedals produce a torque command. The motor produces torque, the torque accelerates the vehicle and the resulting speed is compared with the target. The approach is also called a driver-oriented or causal model [2, 11]. The approach is widely used in EV engineering texts [4, 6]. Its defining features are: • the input is a target, not the actual speed; • the actual speed is an output obtained by integrating the equation of motion; • a driver model is needed to close the loop; • component limits act naturally, so the vehicle can fail to follow the target. 4.2.2 Forward-Looking Model Architecture Figure 4.6 shows the complete model. A drive cycle supplies the reference speed, the driver model compares it with measured speed, and the VCU converts pedal commands into a motor torque command and a friction brake command. The motor controller, inverter and motor then  22

produce torque from battery power. Torque passes through the transmission to the vehicle dynamics block, which outputs speed, fed back along the top of the diagram. The battery also feeds SoC and power limits to the VCU, so that a weak battery reduces performance just as in a real car. It assumes that the vehicle follows the prescribed speed exactly. Starting from that speed, it calculates the force required at the wheels, then the torque and speed at the motor, then the electrical power at the inverter and the battery.  30

Calculations run from the road back to the energy source, hence the name [2, 11]. The method is also called the drive-cycle or quasi-static approach, since each sample is treated as a steady operating point. Its key features are: • the speed profile is an input; there is no driver model; • no differential equation for speed is solved, so there is no speed feedback; • the only integrated quantities are energy and SoC; • demand is assumed to be met, whether or not the hardware can deliver it. Its limitations follow directly: • It cannot show that a car fails to follow a cycle; torque above the motor limit is simply computed. An output check must flag such samples. • Driver and control dynamics are absent, so it cannot be used for tuning controllers or for hardware-in-the-loop tests. • Acceleration from numerical differences depends on sample rate; 1 Hz data hide short peaks. • Thermal and other transient limits must be handled outside the main calculation. 4.3.13 MATLAB/Simulink Implementation of the Backward-Looking Model A backward model is natural in MATLAB as vectorised code, but it can equally be built as open-loop blocks, as in Figure 4.20. Electric Vehicle System Engineering 4.4.2 B24EES502 Why Each Is Useful Backward models for energy studies. Energy depends on the speed trace and the efficiency chain, not on the fine detail of a controller. Since the backward model follows the trace exactly, every candidate design is compared on the same work done at the wheels, and thousands of runs are affordable. For the reference BEV on MIDC, the backward net energy is 1.302 kWh and the forward PI-driver result is 1.289 kWh, a difference of 1%. Tracking the cycle to within about 0.3 km/h rms therefore has little effect on energy. Forward models for control and actual response. Only a causal model has a vehicle that can fall behind its target. If a controller limits torque, a forward model shows the speed falling, the driver pressing harder and the integrator winding up. Pedal mapping, jerk limits, regenerative blending and driveability cannot be studied any other way. 4.4.3 Combined and Hybrid Modelling Approaches ADVISOR combined the two ideas [11, 12]. A backward pass computes what is demanded, a check finds what the components can supply, and a forward pass returns what was actually delivered, as in Figure 4.22. If the limit is not reached, the vehicle follows the trace, retaining the backward model’s speed. If it is reached, the delivered speed replaces the demand, and the trace miss is reported. Other hybrids use a fast backward model for design optimisation and a forward model for final verification, which is the common industrial practice. Gao et al. review these structures in [1]. It stands in for the human, or for the test technician who follows a trace on a dynamometer. Its job is not to imitate a person perfectly, but to generate realistic, repeatable pedal commands that keep the vehicle within an allowed band around the reference. The driver matters in three ways: it closes the speed loop, it sets how aggressively the powertrain is used, and it therefore influences energy consumption and component stress.  40

The brake torque at one wheel is T fr = 2µ p pb A p reff , (4.37) with µ p the pad friction coefficient, pb the line pressure in Pa, A p the piston area in m2 , reff the effective disc radius in m, and 2 for the two faces of the disc. All braking energy becomes heat in the disc. The system is strong and works down to zero speed, but it recovers nothing. 4.6.3 Regenerative Braking and Motor Operation as a Generator In regenerative braking, the inverter commands negative torque. Figure 4.36 shows the process. The wheels drive the rotor, and the inverter sets i∗q < 0 so that stator current opposes the rotation. The torque on the rotor is therefore a braking torque, while the back EMF exceeds the inverter’s fundamental voltage so that power flows toward the DC link. No switch changes state in the machine: the difference between motoring and generating lies solely in the sign of the current command. Wheel drives T m < 0 PMSM rotor e>V Six-switch bridge Ib < 0 DC link, battery i∗q < 0: stator current opposes rotation, so torque is braking and power flows to the DC link Figure 4.36: Motor operating in generator mode. Figure 4.37 shows the battery side. Current enters the positive terminal, so I < 0 by the discharge-positive convention. (4.48) Limits on Regenerative Braking Regenerative torque is available only within several limits, each of which may be the active one. • Motor torque limit. |T m | ≤ T pk (ωm ) on the generator side of the envelope. • Inverter current limit. Phase current cannot exceed the device rating; this acts through the same torque limit. • Battery charge acceptance. Charge power is limited to Pchg (z, Θ), which falls in a high SoC and at low temperature. Lithium plating risk makes cold charging particularly restricted. • Battery SoC limit. Above about 95% SoC regeneration is largely unavailable, for example just after a full charge. • Low-speed limit. Back EMF and power both vanish as ωm → 0, so regeneration fades in below about 5–15 km/h. Friction takes over for the final stop, or the inverter briefly holds torque while drawing a small battery current.  51

• Vehicle stability. Regeneration on one axle can upset the car on slippery roads, so ABS or ESC activation cancels it. • Fault conditions. Electric Vehicle System Engineering 4.6.12 B24EES502 Brake Force Distribution, Front and Rear Axle Braking Deceleration moves load to the front axle. With wheelbase L, CG height hcg and distances l f and lr from the CG to the front and rear axles, axle loads in N for deceleration ad are (︄ )︄ (︄ )︄ mg ad mg ad Fz f = lr + hcg , Fzr = l f − hcg . (4.52) L g L g The ideal distribution divides the brake force in proportion to these loads, so that both axles reach the adhesion limit together. In practice the distribution is kept front-biased, since locking the rear wheels first makes the car unstable. A single front motor can regenerate only through the front axle, and a rear motor only through the rear, so the rear share must stay within stability limits. For a drive axle share β, the regenerative torque cannot exceed βT b∗ without deviating from the intended distribution unless the system permits a safe bias. 4.6.13 ABS Interaction and Brake-by-Wire Systems Under hard braking on a slippery road, ABS modulates pressure at each wheel to hold longitudinal slip near the peak of the friction curve. Regenerative torque acts through a gearbox and has a different dynamic response, so it is usually faded out quickly when ABS activates, leaving control to the hydraulic system. In some designs, the fast motor torque assists the wheel slip control. Brake-by-wire decouples pedal from hydraulics: a sensor reads the pedal, a simulator provides feel, and an electric pump or booster generates pressure. This is what allows the invisible exchange of friction for regenerative torque. In fault conditions, a hydraulic fallback connects the pedal directly to the wheels. 4.6.14 Regenerative Braking under Different Operating Conditions • Urban stop-and-go. Frequent mild stops suit regeneration very well; a large share of traction energy can be recovered. • Highway. Few stops mean drag does the braking, so little energy is available. • Long downhill. Power is available for a long time, so thermal limits and a full battery may end regeneration. Friction brakes must be able to take over. • Cold battery. Charge acceptance is low until the pack warms. • Full battery. Regeneration is reduced or absent just after charging. • Emergency braking. Friction dominates; the tyres set the limit. 4.6.15 Control Algorithms Algorithms 5 to 7 implement the logic above. The first computes capability, the second completes the split so that the demand is met, and the third shares the friction part across the axles.  54

Contactors are open. Key-on and successful self-checks lead to Ready. • Standstill (Ready). High voltage is live with T m∗ = 0, or creep torque in D. • Motoring. Forward traction with T m∗ > 0. • Regenerative braking. Forward motion with T m∗ < 0, entered by a brake press or lift-off. • Reverse. Selected at v ≈ 0. Torque sign reversed and speed limited to a low value. • Fault/limp. Torque is reduced or removed, according to severity. Each arc in the figure carries its guard condition. Transitions between Forward and Reverse require v ≈ 0, because a direct change of sign at speed would shock the driveline. This makes the state machine a safety mechanism as well as a sequencer. 4.7.7 Traction Control Overview Traction control limits wheel slip when torque exceeds what the tyres can transmit. Slip during traction is λ = (ωw rw − v)/(ωw rw ). If λ exceeds about 0.1–0.15, past the peak of the tyre curve, then the VCU reduces torque. An electric motor is much better at this than an engine, because torque can be reduced within a few milliseconds.  62

Forces are in N, speed in m/s and dv/dt in m/s2 . 4.8.5 Rolling Resistance Force A rolling tyre deforms at the contact patch. Material in the tyre wall is compressed and then rebounds, and the rubber returns less energy than it absorbed. This hysteresis shifts the normal force slightly ahead of the wheel centre by a distance e, as seen in Figure 4.57, creating a moment Fz e that opposes rotation. Dividing that moment by the wheel radius gives an equivalent force at the road, Fz e = Crr Fz = Crr mg cos θ, (4.64) Frolling = Fr = rw with Crr = e/rw the dimensionless rolling resistance coefficient. On a small grade cos θ ≈ 1. Crr rises gently with speed and depends on tyre pressure, temperature and road surface. A low-rolling-resistance EV tyre can have a value below 0.008. 4.8.6 Aerodynamic Drag Force Moving air separates from the body, and the wake leaves a pressure deficit behind the car. The drag force is Faero = Fa = 12 ρ Cd A (v + vw )2 , (4.65) where ρ is air density in kg/m3 (about 1.2 at 20◦ C at sea level), Cd is the drag coefficient, A the frontal area in m2 , and vw the head-wind speed in m/s. The product 21 ρv2 is the dynamic pressure in Pa. Dimensionally, kg/m3 ×m2 ×m2 /s2 = kg m/s2 = N. With zero wind, the reference car has Fa = 0.396v2 .  68

Raises rolling, grade and inertial forces in proportion. Regeneration returns part of the inertial energy, but rolling loss is lost. A 10% mass increase raises urban consumption substantially and has less effect on the highway.  75

• Frontal area and drag coefficient. The product Cd A sets highway consumption; power rises with v3 . A 10% reduction in Cd A gives a 10% lower drag power at all speeds. • Wheel radius. A larger radius lowers force for a given wheel torque and lowers motor speed for a given road speed. It is therefore equivalent to a change in G/rw , and must be considered together with the gear ratio. • Rolling resistance. Important at low and moderate speeds, and Pr rises only linearly with speed. Tyre choice is one of the cheapest ways to gain range. Two conditions must be separated. Peak performance is what the car can do for seconds, such as overtaking. Continuous performance is what it can do indefinitely, such as climbing a long hill. Heat decides the difference. Peak ratings are limited by current and voltage, and continuous ratings by temperature. Figure 4.82 shows the sizing architecture: targets become forces, forces become motor and ratio choices, which then flow to inverter and battery ratings, and a drive cycle supplies the thermal duty.  92

A motor can tolerate 30 s or more due to its large thermal mass. An inverter’s capability is limited to seconds. A battery’s peak is commonly specified as a 10 s or 30 s pulse. The overall peak rating is set by the shortest of these, and the BMS or inverter counts down remaining overload time. Safety margins should be added to the final selected rating, not to each intermediate step, or the design will be needlessly oversized. 4.11.12 Powertrain Efficiency Over a cycle, the average efficiency is the ratio of energies, not the product of constant values. Efficiency also depends on sizing: an oversized motor runs at a smaller fraction of rated torque in normal driving, where efficiency tends to be lower. This is a further reason not to oversize. 4.11.13 Sizing Workflow and Algorithm Figure 4.89 gives the sizing workflow. Selecting from continuous power ensures sustained speed, hill climbing and repeatable performance, and it mainly determines the cooling system and machine volume. A correct design meets both: pick the machine whose peak curve covers the acceleration points and whose continuous curve covers the sustained points. Passenger cars tend to be peak-driven, since their duty is mild, while buses and trucks tend to be continuous-driven, because they spend long periods at high load. 4.11.16 MATLAB/Simulink Implementation of Powertrain Sizing Sizing is mostly a script that sweeps design variables, as Figure 4.90 indicates. Its purpose is comparability: every vehicle runs the same trace, so that consumption, emissions and range can be compared. Some  101

In simulation they provide the common input for backward and forward models. A cycle is only a sample of real driving, so a vehicle tuned to a single cycle may perform differently on the road. Regulators therefore moved from NEDC to WLTC, which is more dynamic. 4.12.3 Urban, Highway, Combined and Stop-and-Go Driving Urban driving has low average speed, frequent stops and long idling, so inertial energy dominates. Highway driving has high steady speed and few stops, so aerodynamic drag dominates. Combined driving mixes the two. Stop-and-go driving is the extreme urban case. Acceleration and deceleration levels set the peak power and the regenerative opportunity. A top layer coordinates subsystems and picks set-points. Formulation. rk = S(xk , dk ), where S maps measured state and driver demand into references. Inputs: pedals, modes, limits. Outputs: torque, power and thermal set-points. Feedback: SoC, speed, temperature, faults. Implementation: periodic task on the VCU. Advantages: clear structure, separates concerns. IF-THEN rules chosen from engineering knowledge, as in Figure 4.103. Rules read the inputs, thresholds tune them and the output is a defined action. Formulation. u = gi (x) when condition Ci (x) is true, with the first true condition winning. Inputs: ua , ub , v, z, Θ. Outputs: T m∗ , T fr∗ , flags. Feedback: measured states. Implementation: compare, branch, look up. Advantages: simple, transparent, cheap to verify. Limitations: not optimal, and tuning grows with the number of rules. Computation: very low. It has low to moderate computational load, but requires sufficient excitation to work reliably. Intelligent control covers neural networks, reinforcement learning and related data-driven methods. A reinforcement learning agent learns a policy u = π(x) that maximises reward, for example low energy with good tracking. Such methods can handle complex behaviour, but require extensive data and raise verification challenges, and so most remain in research or in supervisory, non-safety roles. 4.13.14 Control Algorithms Algorithms 24 to 29 summarise the main strategies in a compact form, for comparison with the fuller versions in Sections 4.6 and 4.7.  114

It equals usable energy divided by energy consumption per unit distance. The numerator is mostly a property of the battery, and the denominator a property of the vehicle, driver, route and weather. Range prediction therefore needs to model both, as shown in Figure 4.124. Route, speed, grade and ambient conditions go into a vehicle model to give consumption e. SoC and health determine usable energy Eu . Their ratio is shown to the driver, and the measured consumption continually updates the estimate. Results vary among cycles, because the speed profiles differ. Real-world range depends on actual speed, traffic, terrain, climate and driver. The two can differ widely. A rated MIDC range is typically optimistic relative to real driving, since MIDC is gentle and is run in mild temperature with HVAC off. 4.15.3 Battery Usable, Nominal and Operating Window Nominal energy is Enom = Vnom Q. Uses the equations of this unit. It needs no training data and extrapolates well, but requires parameters and route information [31]. • Drive-cycle-based prediction. Selects or builds a representative cycle for the expected trip, then simulates it. • Historical energy consumption methods. These use the average over recent kilometres, emeas = ∆E/∆D. This is the simple “guess-o-meter” in many cars, which reacts slowly to route changes. • Statistical prediction. Fits distributions of consumption to trip features, giving a range with confidence bounds.  127

• Regression-based prediction. Fits a function such as e = β0 + β1 v2 + β2 /v + β3 s + β4 Paux by least squares. The terms are chosen from physics, which improves extrapolation. • Machine learning-based prediction. Random forests and gradient boosting learn nonlinear mappings from trip features to e [29]. • Neural network-based range prediction. Networks, including recurrent ones, process speed and battery time series, and need a lot of data. • Hybrid physics and data-driven prediction. A physics model gives the baseline ephys and a learned term corrects the residual, e = ephys +gθ (x). This retains physical plausibility while capturing unmodelled effects. Table 4.31 compares the two families. Physics-based models are explainable and need parameters. Data-driven models adapt to the fleet and need data. Hybrid methods try to take the best of each. A balance at each interface like this is the best verification of a model, as it shows at once if a loss is missing or double counted.
